## BOX 11 | Ahmedabad's TDR-enabled redevelopment to revitalize public housing and slums

In Ahmedabad, 43 slum redevelopment projects covering 8.2 hectares of land and 12 public housing redevelopment projects covering 4.8 hectares of land were undertaken using Transferable Development Rights (TDR). Under the redevelopment norms, each site is required to be equipped with community infrastructure such as Anganwadis, health centers, gardens, solar panels, sewage treatment plants, and rainwater harvesting systems, ensuring a sustainable living environment. The land for these projects is owned by the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), and the beneficiaries are chosen through a lottery system. Projects on municipal land allocate full ownership to beneficiaries via transparent selection processes, ensure a 40 percent increase in carpet area for residential units and 25 percent for commercial units in public housing redevelopment, and provide interim rent support, combining tenure security with improved standards.

Ahmedabad's experience shows that In-Situ Slum Redevelopment (ISSR)-type projects can serve the public interest rather than purely private interests when they embed community participation and continuous learning. Long-standing collaboration between the Municipal Corporation and intermediaries such as Mahila Housing Trust has helped refine standard operating procedures (SOPs) and request for proposals (RFPs), raise design and amenity standards, and ensure developer accountability, because they can utilize TDR benefits only after the building permission and building use certificate for the slum rehabilitation component have been issued. Challenges persist regarding operations and maintenance issues, interim rent payments, and the acceptance of larger units by residents, the areas of which may be less than the areas they currently occupy owing to illegal extensions.

Source: National Urban Conclave 2025 Livestream | Breakout Session: Housing 2025; Patel and Varma 2025.

Ahmedabad's experience shows that ISSR-type projects can serve the public interest rather than purely private interests when they embed community participation and continuous learning (see Box 11).

Land and housing market reforms must prioritize modernizing land and property systems to enable secure, low-cost transactions and efficient use of urban land. Key actions include end-to-end digitization of land records, streamlined registration and permitting, and harmonization of municipal databases to allow rapid verification of ownership and land use, which can reduce disputes, unlock underused parcels, and lower transaction costs (PIB 2023a).

Reforming rental and tenure frameworks is essential to bring vacant and informally held units into productive use. Implementing and adapting the Model Tenancy Act, combined with improved title clarity and faster dispute resolution, can encourage property owners to enter the formal rental market and expand options for low-income renters (Gandhi et al. 2021).

Improving transparency and reducing legal risk in real estate transactions can help correct price distortions and build buyer confidence. Measures such as strengthening litigation disclosure requirements, enhancing enforcement under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, and standardizing information on project approvals and land titles can create more predictable conditions for both buyers and smaller developers (Tandel et al. 2023).

Tamil Nadu, a highly urbanized and industrialized state, offers a strong example of how a state-backed fund can de-risk and scale private participation in affordable housing through the Tamil Nadu Shelter Fund (TNSF). It finances affordable rental and ownership projects for EWS, LIG, industrial workers, women, students, senior citizens, and migrant workers, while being managed by a professional fund manager—the Tamil Nadu Infrastructure Fund Management Company (TNIFMC), in which the state government holds a 49 percent stake (see Box 12).

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 137

## BOX 12 | Delivering affordable rental housing through the Tamil Nadu Shelter Fund

The Tamil Nadu Shelter Fund (TNSF) was established as a private equity fund dedicated to investing in affordable and sustainable housing projects across the state. It was launched as a $92 million fund, comprising $22 million contributed by the Tamil Nadu Housing Board and the state government, and $35 million each from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the World Bank. The fund serves as a de-risking instrument to attract greater private-sector participation. TNSF operates as a financial intermediary that provides risk capital to special-purpose vehicles and other entities serving segments excluded from formal housing markets. By retaining demand risk with industrial employers in worker housing, leveraging public land and dedicated SPVs for working women's hostels, and outsourcing facility management to private operators under clear standards, TNSF aligns incentives while mandating Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and green certification to embed sustainability alongside affordability. By November 2025, TNSF had supported around 27,000 affordable rental beds, achieved green certification for roughly 2 million square feet of built space, benefited approximately 20,000 women, and helped create about 15,000 jobs across Tamil Nadu. By FY2028, the fund expects to complete 54 projects, pointing to the potential of well-designed, state-anchored investment vehicles to crowd in private capital for inclusive housing.

Source: National Urban Conclave 2025 Livestream | Breakout Session: Housing 2025, The World Bank.

## Challenge 3

### **Policies for resilient low-income housing and slum upgrading continue to prioritize the physical structure of the house over the resilience of the wider settlement and the systems that deliver basic services.**

Although policy language now emphasizes “disaster-resilient” and “climate-smart” housing, implementation remains narrowly focused on building materials and compliance with structural codes, with far less attention paid to where settlements are located, how they are serviced, and how risks are managed at neighborhood scale (Dodman et al. 2023). Weak enforcement of standards in informal and peripheral areas, limited integration of livelihoods and tenure security into resilience efforts, and fragmented mandates across housing, disaster management, and state agencies further reinforce this structure-centric bias (World Bank Group 2025a).

Emerging debates in research and practice argue for a shift from this house-by-house approach to a settlement- and system-centric perspective that treats resilience as a function of site, layout, and infrastructure networks as much as walls and roofs. This means planning for the siting of low-income housing in relation to urban heat islands (UHIs), natural drainage channels, mobility networks, social infrastructure, and evolving climate hazards, particularly for the urban poor and in fast-growing peri-urban corridors. Current policies continue to reflect the legacy of viewing slums primarily as illegal or unhygienic spaces to be cleared, which has driven evictions and relocation rather than in situ improvement (Bhan 2009; Kapoor and Chakma 2024). As a result, access to climate-resilient services such as treated water, safe sanitation, reliable electricity, and all-weather drainage remains far worse in slums than in formal neighborhoods (Singh and Roy 2020; Mukherjee et al. 2021). Moreover, in high-risk locations such as floodplains, unsafe industrial edges, and highly polluted sites, in situ upgrading alone is often insufficient, and carefully planned relocation through sites-and-services approaches can provide a viable, climate-responsive alternative. Drawing on longitudinal evidence from World Bank-supported sites-and-services projects in Chennai and Mumbai, Owens et al. (2018) show that, under the right design and locational conditions, initially under-occupied serviced plots evolved over two decades into compact, mixed-use, mixed-income neighborhoods with high levels of incremental investment by low-income households.

Because slums are informal and politically marginal, they are disproportionately located on ecologically fragile or degraded lands—beside rail lines, nalas, and water bodies in core areas, or near landfills and polluting industries on the periphery—where exposure to flooding, landslides, heat, and pollution is highest (Rangwala et al. 2024).

Underserved settlements are thus doubly disadvantaged: they face greater climate hazards and lack robust service systems and public investment to help them adapt (Pandey et al. 2018). In many informal settlements, indoor temperatures exceed already extreme outdoor heat because of heat-trapping materials and poor ventilation (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2021), and studies show they can be several degrees hotter than adjacent formal housing, illustrating how service and planning deficits translate directly into climate risk (Chatterjee 2020).

Ex situ rehabilitation schemes often compound these vulnerabilities by placing resettlement housing on the urban fringe in locations chosen for low land value rather than safety, serviceability, climate resilience, or access to social networks. These “non-prime” sites tend to have weaker environmental oversight (Mani and Wajih 2021), higher levels of pollution and waste dumping, and limited basic services, contributing to significantly worse health outcomes and lower life expectancy for relocated communities than for residents of better-located inner-city slums (Goswami and Basak 2021). Evidence of greater deprivation and disparity in peripheral slums than in city cores (Singh and Roy 2020) underscores that the central policy challenge is not just to build stronger houses but to upgrade entire settlements and service systems, thereby embedding resilience in the everyday environments of low-income residents.

## Recommendation 3

### **Promote climate resilient, infrastructure-integrated slum upgrades.**

National housing policy should move beyond a narrow focus on stronger individual houses to programs that upgrade entire settlements and service systems in climate-safe, well-connected locations. Climate resilience needs to be built into slum upgrades as a core objective, by treating informal settlements as priority sites for integrated investments in land tenure security, basic services, blue-green infrastructure, and risk-informed planning, rather than as areas to be cleared or relocated. Well-located, affordable serviced plots with small plot sizes, efficient site planning, and provision for mixed uses and social amenities are an important policy option alongside in situ upgrading in cases where climate risk remains high and livable densities cannot reasonably be achieved in existing slum locations.

A first step is to explicitly align major housing and urban missions—such as NMSH 2.0 and PMAY-U—around settlement-level resilience outcomes, with special attention to informal housing and SMTs that have limited adaptive capacity. Program guidelines should require that slum

140 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

upgrading packages combine secure, appropriate forms of tenure; all-weather access to treated water, sanitation, drainage, electricity, and waste management; and energy-efficient, low-carbon service delivery. Blue-green measures such as permeable paving, stormwater drains, groundwater recharge structures, and shaded open spaces should be standard elements, not add-ons, in hazard-prone settlements.

Odisha's JAGA Mission illustrates how such an approach can work in practice, by coupling land rights with a defined bundle of infrastructure and public space improvements in climate-exposed slums (see Box 13). Building on this experience, national policy should encourage states to design upgrading programs that map climate hazards and service gaps across informal and formal housing; prioritize slums located in high-risk zones; and embed community participation in deciding how multipurpose infrastructure (for example, community centers that can double as shelters) is designed and located. At the same time, systematic, disaggregated data collection on climate impacts, housing conditions, and access to services is needed to understand differential vulnerability and track how upgrading shifts risk over time.

Finally, climate-resilient slum upgrades should be framed as a long-term urban transformation agenda rather than a one-off project. This means ring-fencing dedicated climate and urban funds for upgrading, tying city-level climate and disaster plans to concrete upgrading pipelines, and building the capacity of ULGs and community organizations to plan, implement, and maintain resilient infrastructure in informal settlements.

### BOX 13 | Odisha's slum upgrading program helped build habitable, climate-resilient settlements

Odisha's slum upgrading program has demonstrated how securing land rights and investing in basic services can create more habitable, climate-resilient settlements. Through the Odisha Land Rights to Slum Dwellers Act, 2017, landless urban slum residents receive inheritable, non-transferable titles, providing a foundation of tenure security (Department of Housing & Urban Affairs, Government of Odisha 2023). This is implemented alongside the Odisha Liveable Habitat Mission (JAGA Mission), which upgrades slums and delists them by delivering a package of nine core amenities: piped water, stormwater drainage, individual toilets, electricity, street lighting, permeable street paving, open spaces with groundwater recharge structures, children's play areas, and micro-activity centers.

These interventions target settlements that are highly exposed to cyclones, floods, heat waves, and droughts along Odisha's 480 km coastline, helping residents secure services most likely to be disrupted during climate events and strengthening everyday resilience. Subsidies enable households to build more permanent structures that are better able to withstand extreme weather.

In JAGA's pilot phase, beneficiaries included the Nolia migrant fishing community, which lives in high-cyclone-risk zones and faces acute socioeconomic disadvantages. The community's participation shaped climate-resilient design: whereas most multipurpose community centers known as parichaya are open structures, the Nolia settlement requested a walled parichaya so it could function as a cyclone shelter, showing how slum upgrading can jointly address risk and improve living conditions.

Source: Chakrabarty 2022.

## CHAPTER 8.

# Economic Development and Inclusive Growth

The chapter examines how economic policies and urbanization pathways can be better aligned while reducing inequity, gender, and generational gaps. Key challenges and recommendations include the need to address unplanned urban sprawl, which results in productivity losses; the rise of informal low-wage employment amidst increasing inequality; and the inadequacies of industrial clusters and SEZs in balancing broader regional growth with a reduction in inequality and improvements in sustainability. Fragmented migration policy, multiple deprivations faced by urban youth, and persistently low female workforce participation, compounded by neglect of care work, further undermine equitable and demographically sustainable urban development.

![img-10.jpeg](img-10.jpeg)

![img-11.jpeg](img-11.jpeg)

Urbanization has traditionally been closely associated with economic growth and industrialization (Harris and Todaro 1970; Kuznets 1955). However, India's economic growth since the 1980s has decoupled from its urbanization rates, which have remained relatively low or even declined (see Figure 30). A significant portion of India's urbanization occurs in rural-to-urban transition zones through dispersed peri-urban growth that is often unrecorded in official statistics. This “hidden urbanization” (see the discussion in Chapter 3) features a shift from agricultural to nonfarm livelihoods. One key factor is the ruralization of manufacturing, where industries have increasingly shifted to rural areas, leading to a lack of formal employment opportunities in urban centers (see Figure 31). The lack of formal job creation in urban areas has hindered the structural transformation typically associated with urbanization, where people move from low-productivity rural activities to higher-productivity urban jobs (Mohan 2025). Between 1991 and 2021, India's population grew by

about 60 percent (growing at an annual exponential growth rate of 1.56 percent), but manufacturing's GDP share remained stagnant (it hovered between 14 and 17 percent during this period) (World Bank Group 2024a), while the capital-intensive services sector (Deng et al. 2005), especially information technology, expanded rapidly. This has led to informal, low-income urban jobs with insecure incomes, contributing to inequality and challenging equitable resource distribution (Sen 2019). Moreover, service-sector growth in India is primarily experienced in high-density clusters in cities such as Hyderabad, Chennai, and Mumbai, which have seen significant growth in services due to agglomeration economies and knowledge spillovers. These high-density locations continue to attract service industries, while medium-density cities struggle to grow due to barriers such as poor infrastructure and limited access to telecommunication services (Desmet et al. 2013).

Despite the slow pace of urbanization and lack of formal job creation in urban areas, Indian cities contribute around 54 percent of the country's GDP (2011–12) and account for 48 percent of employment (MoSPI 2014). Only 10 cities account for nearly 30 percent of India's national GDP (World Bank and Asian Development Bank 2025), and this concentration underscores the importance of urban areas to the nation's economic progress. However, about 32 percent of urban areas lies outside official city limits, reflecting unplanned expansion (World Bank and Asian Development Bank 2025) that inevitably leads to poor service delivery, increased environmental risks, and lower productivity. In Indian cities, labor-intensive industries are now usually located outside core urban areas. They have flocked to peri-urban and rural areas, attracted by looser environmental and zoning restrictions, cheaper land, lower wages, and operational costs, leaving behind cities, where employment generation in the organized sector lags behind that in the informal sector (Mohan 2025). Firms opt to stay informal and under the regulatory radar. At the same time, informality traps them in a low-performance–low-dynamism cycle (Mathur et al. 2021). Entrepreneurism, too, has settled into a low-level equilibrium. The vast majority of workers in the informal sector, many of them migrants, are excluded from most benefits in cities, including access to social security programs, and many live in overcrowded slums (Rajan and Bhagat 2021).

Cities enable human development, and investment in human capital is fundamental for inclusive growth, because it enhances individuals' capacity to participate in economic activities, and thus allows economic benefits to be shared more equitably across the population (Alexander 2015). Effective urban policies focusing on inclusive growth can improve human development outcomes (OECD 2016). A human development approach to urban policy fosters greater opportunities for people living in cities to lead meaningful lives. It uses economic growth as a means toward this end, rather than viewing it as an end in itself (Stewart et al. 2018). This requires better policies for firm-level economic activity as well as for human development. Many urban workers remain in informal jobs with inadequate social safety nets, affordable housing, and access to basic services such as sanitation, health care, and public transportation. A human development approach to urbanization policies, emphasizing inclusive growth and better social protections, is essential to ensure that economic benefits are broadly shared amid growing informal employment.

The Global State of National Urban Policy 2024 survey in 78 countries found that half the respondents gave extensive attention to “inclusive growth and opportunities for all” (OECD and UN-Habitat 2024). This category has four action tracks, and this chapter focuses on one of them: “Provide opportunities for all urban residents,

146

WRI-INDIA.ORG

particularly by ensuring that urban development is sensitive to vulnerable urban populations. Promote diversity and inclusion, reduce gender and/or generational gaps.”

Despite India’s atypical urbanization trajectory, decoupled from national economic growth and characterized by dispersed peri-urbanization, urban areas remain central to economic productivity, employment generation, and structural transformation. The Union Budget 2025–26 reflects this essential linkage through increased outlays for urban development, introducing three important policy measures:

- Urban Challenge Fund: A Challenge Fund of INR 1 trillion has been earmarked to implement the proposals for “Cities as Growth Hubs,” “Creative Redevelopment of Cities,” and “Water and Sanitation.”
- National Geospatial Mission: To develop foundational geospatial infrastructure and data for informed urban planning.
- Strengthening Urban Livelihoods: A scheme for the socioeconomic upliftment of urban workers will be implemented.

Further, India’s policy landscape for economic development in cities and rapidly urbanizing regions is shaped by the action of several central ministries and planning bodies. Table 16 outlines the strategic policy approaches across the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, MoHUA, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Ministry of MSME, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and NITI Aayog. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry recognizes urbanization as an opportunity for economic expansion and invests heavily in city-centric industrial and logistical infrastructure. Its Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) has instituted industrial corridors, the Make in India and Start-up India initiatives, the PM GatiShakti program, and Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes to stimulate manufacturing capacities, attract FDI, and foster urban industrial clusters (Ministry of Commerce and Industry 2025). MoHUA prioritizes technology-enabled urban planning, efficient transportation, clean infrastructure for sustainable urbanization, and improved governance of cities for inclusive economic growth (MoHUA 2020). The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare encourages region-specific planning adaptable to urbanizing peri-urban regions and leverages large domestic markets. Micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) policy reforms focus on easing access to credit, simplifying regulatory processes, including marginalized groups, and fostering urban entrepreneurial ecosystems through tech upgrades and support for urban and peri-urban MSMEs, particularly in the start-up and advanced manufacturing spaces (IIFL Finance 2024). MeitY, through the Digital India and

e-Kranti initiatives, aims to integrate information and communication technology (ICT) across urban service delivery, governance, and economic activity, enabling smart urban economies and seamless digital public infrastructure (Department of Electronics and Information 2015). NITI Aayog, through its Growth Hubs initiative, is steering high-level urban economic strategy for city regions to unlock investment, enhance productivity, and foster innovative city clusters. Despite many policies and initiatives, there are several gaps between intended outcomes (as outlined in India’s National Urban Policy Framework [NUPF] of 2020) and actual progress. The challenges stem from the need for coordination across ministries, states, and a constellation of local agencies, compounded by differences in resource allocation, institutional strength, and the pace of urban growth (NITI Aayog n.d.).

In 2014, NITI Aayog, which replaced the Planning Commission, highlighted that although Indian citizens lived in one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, they lacked minimum basic services. It pointed to low tax revenues, high youth unemployment, and untapped potential to leverage the demographic dividend. It stressed the need to improve the quality of life in urban areas and create vibrant land markets. It proposed transferring authority over land conversion from the revenue department to agencies managing urbanization and making land ownership titles accurate and conclusive to address the paradox of vacant properties in Indian cities in the context of unmet demand for housing. These concerns point to the broader challenge of urban economic development, in which the spatial organization of cities, the functioning of land and housing markets, labor market outcomes, and access to services are closely interlinked and jointly shape productivity, inclusion, and long-term growth.

# Challenges and Recommendations

## Challenge 1

**Spatially uneven, unplanned, and unmanaged growth of cities in India causes productivity loss and imposes additional costs due to the associated negative externalities.**

The mere expansion of UAs does not necessarily mean that agglomeration benefits will flow automatically; the peripheries of large cities are undergoing rapid, unmanaged transformations, resulting in the growth of slums, unauthorized and nonconforming land developments, and inadequate provisions for infrastructure, utilities, and public transport. Industrial firms are increasingly relocating to peripheral areas, contributing to de-industrialization inside cities, increasing the strain on peripheral infrastructure, services, and the natural environment (Dinesh et al. 2016). In this context, unmanaged sprawl, fragmented governance, and inadequate infrastructure in expanding peripheries result in congestion, heat stress, air pollution, flooding losses, and weak public transport, which erode the very productivity benefits that urban density is supposed to provide, especially for low-income workers, migrants, and informal settlements (see Box 14). Urban characteristics such as the availability of infrastructure; geographic location of public facilities, housing, and educational and health services; and industrial structure play a significant role in determining a city's productivity and employment opportunities. Environmental rules introduced between 1980 and 2005 pushed hazardous industries out of metropolitan cores and into suburban and peri-urban zones. There was, however, no assessment of the levels of risk posed by different categories of these industries. This led to the de-industrialization of core city areas (Dinesh et al. 2016). To fully harness the potential of urbanization for creating productive cities, it is essential to address the challenges related to urban planning, infrastructure, and public service delivery (Hasan et al. 2017).

Cities with larger populations tend to have more formal jobs (in firms with 10 or more workers), but higher city density can reduce employment due to congestion effects (Hasan et al. 2017). New evidence suggests that India's service sector exhibits strong agglomeration economies only in very high-density locations—large metropolitan cores and a few specialized clusters—while medium-density cities perform worse than both low- and high-density areas, the opposite of the pattern observed in advanced economies (Desmet et al. 2013).

Aligning economic development with infrastructure-integrated urban planning requires addressing the challenges posed by fragmented governance in

metropolitan areas. Rapidly urbanizing cities such as Bengaluru are characterized by significant fluidity in both spatial organization and governance. The presence of multiple overlapping agencies creates unclear jurisdictions and competition among authorities, weakening accountability. Peripheral zones function as economic engines for many migrants and gig workers—often women and informal sector workers—who work there but typically do not live in these areas. Many of these peripheral areas lie outside formal urban planning frameworks and lack adequate infrastructure, public transport, and workforce protections (Anand et al. 2018). Local governments in these transitional regions have limited power, because the state retains control over land, infrastructure, and industry, frequently delegating regulatory functions to state-controlled parastatal bodies. This power imbalance results in uneven development. Some rural areas receive overlapping funding, while transitioning urban peripheries are often underfunded, restricting the inclusiveness and productive potential of urbanization.

## Recommendation 1

**Align economic development, spatial planning, and infrastructure investment to spur regional growth and leverage the benefits of agglomeration.**

It is essential to align economic development, spatial planning, and infrastructure investment (McVeigh 2024), allowing resources to be directed efficiently and enterprises to thrive in environments tailored to their needs. This alignment requires good-quality infrastructure and amenities, including transportation. The current policy push for growth hubs adopts this approach (see Box 15).

Central and state government manufacturing policies should adopt a more granular socioeconomic perspective at the city agglomeration level. This involves accounting for the specific and varied occupational composition of regions and the barriers to employment, and considering socioeconomic realities and the potential economic advantages of locating industries in particular areas. Spatial mapping of disaggregated data on economic activities across a region can aid this process. The sectoral and industrial makeup, along with the locational characteristics of an urban area, must be studied in order to plan for growth. Industries and firms must be positioned in optimal locations to ensure strong linkages with markets, labor, and capital.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 149

BOX 14 | Snapshot of sector-specific productivity losses from different cities

### Traffic congestion

Studies from Bengaluru indicate significant losses of up to 707,000 productive hours annually, costing around INR 11.7 billion due to traffic jams.$^{a}$ In New Delhi, productivity losses from congestion reach $7,410 million per year, with 85 percent of this cost attributed to buses, underscoring the public infrastructure’s inadequacy. By 2030, congestion costs in New Delhi are projected to rise by 70 percent.$^{b}$

### Heat stress

Rising temperatures in the dense, poorly planned urban environments of Indian cities result in lower average labor productivity. Productivity losses due to heat stress are further compounded by increased incidences of illnesses and fatigue, leading to increased absenteeism.$^{c}$ The differential vulnerability of heat exposure in Indian cities means that inner-city slums and the sprawling, underserved peri-urban settlements are hotter than the rural surroundings.$^{d}$ Extreme heat currently causes 4 percent of New Delhi’s total economic output to be lost due to reduced worker productivity, and this lost output may rise to 5 percent by 2050.$^{e}$ Construction workers in Chennai working outdoors with moderate and heavy workload experienced productivity losses of 18–35 percent.$^{f}$

### Air pollution

In 2019, 17.8 percent of all deaths in India were due to air pollution (including ambient particulate matter pollution, household air pollution, and ambient ozone pollution), and the economic losses due to lost output amounted to 1.3 percent of the GDP.$^{g}$ Big cities and metropolitan areas such as Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata are more susceptible to a significant number of premature deaths due to air pollution.$^{h}$ The economic loss due to lost output from premature deaths and morbidity (attributable to ambient particulate matter pollution) as a percentage of the country’s GDP was 0.84 percent, while this loss for Delhi was estimated to be 1.06 percent.$^{i}$ In particular, the effects of air pollution$^{j}$ are more deeply felt in labor-intensive manufacturing industries such as garment making, causing wages to fall as marginal worker productivity declines due to an increase in pollution.$^{k}$

### Urban flooding and waterlogging

Pluvial urban flooding in India is primarily driven by the encroachment of urban development on flood plains; the increase in impervious surfaces, leading to greater runoff; and the inability of drainage systems to cope with higher precipitation due to climate change.$^{l}$ The cost of damage to municipal infrastructure in Mumbai in the aftermath of a flooding event in 2005$^{m}$ was estimated to be $55 million, with the estimates of total direct damage, including private and commercial buildings, being in the range of $690–1,910 million.$^{n}$ The decline in value added after this event was 1.4 percent of the annual GDP for the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.$^{o}$ Monetary losses from uninsured damage indicate that the average total losses were 3.5–4.5 times a family’s income, with low-income households suffering even greater losses—those below the poverty line faced damage-related monetary losses amounting to six times their monthly income.$^{p}$

The new CER scheme in the 2026–27 Union Budget directly reinforces this chapter’s call to align economic development, spatial planning, and infrastructure investment at the scale of city regions rather than individual municipalities. By mapping CERs based on specific growth drivers and allocating around INR 50 billion per region over five years through reform- and results-linked challenge-based funding, the budget operationalizes a place-based, agglomeration-oriented approach similar to the Growth Hubs blueprint in the previous budget. This budget, however, places greater emphasis on Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities and temple towns, which have historically been underserved.

Nevertheless, challenge- and results-based funding can unintentionally privilege already well-resourced city regions and well-organized economic actors, while leaving behind smaller ULGs, peri-urban panchayats, informal settlements, women workers, and micro-enterprises that lack the bandwidth to compete for funds or to document “bankable” outcomes. To mitigate these risks, an NUP could encourage an incremental approach in which CER challenge windows are paired with dedicated technical assistance, pre-financing for weaker jurisdictions, minimum inclusion safeguards for low-income neighborhoods and informal workers, and explicit criteria to ensure that at least a share of CER investments flows to capacity-constrained small towns and transitional areas within each region.

Detailed spatial studies, such as the 2023 study of Delhi’s National Capital Region (NCR), provide critical insights into inclusive economic development in city regions. The study highlights the importance of identifying industries benefiting from locational advantages such as proximity to resources, skilled labor, or markets within agglomerations

(Mathews et al. 2023). It underscores the need for balanced development strategies that prevent economic decline in core areas while supporting growth in peripheral zones, which require infrastructure, services, and public transport to sustain urbanization. Revitalizing core cities calls for policies such as industrial reforms, infrastructure upgrades, mixed-use development, and private-sector partnerships, while peri-urban areas should leverage their manufacturing strengths through sustainable, planned urbanization.

Successful enterprises need space to grow. However, very often, once a firm grows beyond a certain size, it does not have any option but to relocate into the periphery. Policy measures should focus on allowing such choices to be dictated by market forces rather than by regulatory fiat. Land-use and zoning norms should therefore be more flexible in order to allow non-hazardous, non-nuisance-creating industries to grow in line with economic forces. An integrated approach combining economic geography insights with governance reforms and adaptive land-use policies can promote balanced, inclusive, productive, and sustainable urbanization.

#### BOX 15 | Growth Hubs Initiative with economic strategy driving spatial planning

The Growth Hubs Initiative by the government provides a good blueprint for economic-development-led urban planning. It does not restrict urban planning to city boundaries but encompasses the whole region. The initiative seeks to develop holistic economic plans based on three pillars:

- An economic and investment plan
- Quality of life
- An inclusivity and sustainability plan

It moves away from a reactive approach toward managing urbanization to a proactive approach with economic strategy as a driver of spatial planning. Growth Hubs policies have been planned in four city regions—Mumbai, Surat, Varanasi, and Visakhapatnam—with other cities to be included in the future.

Source: NITI Aayog 2024.

## Challenge 2

### A predominantly informal, low-wage urban labor market is locking workers into precarity while constraining the inclusive growth potential of MSMEs.

Post-1992 studies of urbanization and growth in India have pointed to the urbanization of poverty, accompanied by the informalization of the urban economy (Datt et al. 2016). Analysis of Periodic Labour Force Survey 2023-24 data shows that informal employment (comprising those working in the informal sector, i.e., all “proprietary and partnership enterprises,” as also defined by The National Sample Survey Organisation) made up nearly 68 percent of India’s entire urban workforce. Informal workers earn less and have less job security than formal workers, and instead of the expected inverse correlation between per capita income and informality, India’s informal sector is expected to continue expanding as its economy grows (La Porta and Shleifer 2014). The study on Delhi’s economic geography discussed in the previous section found that although Delhi NCR is India’s foremost economic agglomeration with high infrastructure provision and decentralized jobs, the economic transformation of Delhi NCR has seen increasing unemployment, decreasing female workforce participation, and access to only the most menial jobs for marginalized groups (Mathews et al. 2023). These findings raise questions about how productive the region really is and for whom. A deeper understanding will be required to craft diverse, targeted policy responses for more inclusive economic development in the region.

The Periodic Labour Force Survey 2023-24 (see Figure 32) shows that the agricultural sector’s labor force has the largest proportion of informal workers (96 percent), followed by construction (93 percent). Of the total urban informal workforce (Figure 33), wholesale and retail trade comprises the maximum at nearly 26 percent, followed by manufacturing at 21 percent, construction at 14 percent, and agriculture at 9.5 percent. Thus, urban informal employment is concentrated in labor-intensive, low-productivity sectors such as construction, manufacturing, and agriculture, and in wholesale and retail trade, which largely comprises working owners, informally hired workers, and unpaid family members (NITI Aayog 2025).

In urban India, gig work contributes to the growth of informal employment by absorbing the underemployed population. Estimates from NITI Aayog indicate that the gig workforce is expected to rise from 7.7 million in 2020 to 23.5 million by 2029–30 (NITI Aayog 2022). However, gig workers face challenges such as precarious working conditions, income instability, lack of social security benefits, algorithmic management, and limited worker rights. Gig work often operates outside formal regulatory systems, lacking formal contracts, social security, and paid leave (Sahu and Behera 2025).

City size is inversely correlated with the share of informal employment. SMTs witness higher levels of informal employment as the workforce transitions from farm to nonfarm employment. The highest share of formal labor is found in ICT and finance (see Figure 34). In SMTs (stratas 1–3), the manufacturing and construction sectors remain predominantly informal, whereas in larger cities (stratum 4) we see a higher percentage of formal employment, suggesting a higher incidence of informality in smaller towns.

Skilled labor is more likely to be employed in formal high-productivity service sectors in urban areas. The urban tertiary sector—particularly ICT, finance and insurance, and real estate services—absorbs high proportions of “skilled” (graduate or higher) labor in formal and informal enterprises (see Table 17). At the same time, formal labor in urban manufacturing is also “skilled,” with 41 percent being graduates or higher. However, the scenario in the informal sector is not as promising, with only 12 percent being graduates and 11 percent finishing high school.

Wage inequality between skilled and unskilled workers in the manufacturing sector has risen during the post-reform period (since 1991) (Papola and Kannan 2017). Whereas casual wage labor in the informal workforce in services such as ICT, finance, real estate, and other tertiary sectors is as low as 0–5 percent, this proportion is as high as 69 percent in the construction sector (see Figure 35). The wages of casual workers have grown at a slower rate than that of regular workers—that is, salaried individuals—who earned several times more wages than casual workers to begin with (Papola and Kannan 2017).

MSMEs are among the largest sources of nonfarm employment in India and are central to stimulating economic growth and generating employment. According to the Economic Survey of 2024-25, MSMEs have reported employing about 230 million people. In 2022–23, the MSME sector accounted for just over 30 percent of India’s GDP, 36 percent of manufacturing, and 45 percent of exports (Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 2024). An increasingly informal, low-wage urban labor market both shapes and constrains MSME-led growth, because MSMEs rely heavily on casual, under-protected workers while also offering one of the few pathways for nonfarm employment and potential formalization in smaller towns and city regions.

## Recommendation 2

### **Strengthen urban livelihood policies to support and formalize India's informal workforce through MSME promotion, green job creation, skilling, and inclusive economic growth.**

Urban policies must explicitly recognize and integrate informal workers, who sustain Indian cities—including street vendors, construction workers, transport operators, domestic workers, waste pickers, and home-based workers—by guaranteeing their legal access to public space, basic services, and public procurement channels. Evidence synthesized in the World Resources Report (Mahindra et al. 2021) underscores that informal work is central to urban economic productivity and household survival. However, it remains largely invisible or marginalized in planning and economic strategies. This situation calls for a “double-pronged” approach of recognizing, reducing, and redistributing the risks and burdens borne by informal workers while expanding their rights and protections (Chen and Beard 2018). In India, this shift is beginning to be institutionalized through measures such as the National Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014, which mandates street vending plans, Town Vending Committees, and legal vending zones, and through city-level experiments such as Pune’s collaboration between civil society organizations (CSOs) and the Municipal Corporation to negotiate vendor spaces, waste-picker integration, and access to social protection in ways that link livelihood security with more orderly, inclusive use of urban public space.

To address the large informal workforce in India, urban policies must prioritize skilling, improving working conditions, protection, and access to services for informal workers while ensuring that those transitioning to formal employment are well equipped to do so. Strengthening Urban Livelihood Missions and City Livelihood Cells can connect informal workers with legitimate economic opportunities through MSMEs, contractors, gig employers, platforms, SHGs, and industrial clusters. Skill academies aligned with local industries and focused education programs are critical for informing disadvantaged communities about their entitlements and training opportunities (Mehrotra 2018). Furthermore, home-worker integration units can help formalize home-based workers by providing credit access, market linkages, and registration assistance (Srivastava and Mehta 2021).

Urban policies need to enhance MSMEs’ operating environment by ensuring market access, improving infrastructure, and simplifying regulatory frameworks to reduce bureaucratic hurdles and operational costs. For instance, Delhi’s Municipal Corporation reform allowing factory owners with MSME registration certificates to use their property tax receipt as a factory license simplifies

compliance and reduces rent-seeking, likely enhancing local employability (Singh 2025). Such measures foster stronger formalization pathways for informal workers engaged in MSME activities. In addition, MSMEs are highly vulnerable to climate-related challenges such as heat, flooding, and supply-chain disruptions, with risks concentrated in dense, infrastructure-poor industrial clusters and among low-income migrant workers. The Growth Hubs analysis for Surat illustrates how deeply climate risk is embedded in the business models, labor conditions, and locations of Indian MSMEs, and why resilience needs to be treated as a competitive issue rather than a secondary concern (see Box 16).

Green jobs in peri-urban areas present significant opportunities for sustainable development and inclusive economic growth. These jobs in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, waste management, urban farming, and green infrastructure are labor intensive and can generate substantial employment (Nain and Chakravorty 2023), especially benefiting marginalized communities and migrant workers. Strengthening rural–urban linkages to provide access to urban markets for peri-urban goods can increase income potential and support local economic systems (Denis and Zérah 2014). Well-planned expansion of urban boundaries, early investment in infrastructure, and provision of knowledge and incentives for urban agriculture will foster green job creation.

Reducing inequality requires tackling multidimensional poverty, ensuring universal access to basic services such as health and education, and creating jobs. Urban employment guarantee schemes linked to public works, housing, and climate-resilient infrastructure demonstrate potential to generate employment while addressing urban development needs (Banerji et al. 2021). The Indira Gandhi Shahari Rozgar Yojana (IGSRY) and the Mukhya Mantri Karma Tatpara Abhiyan (MUKTA) scheme in Odisha have effectively used urban employment guarantees to repair and maintain public housing, accelerate slum upgrades, and create climate-resilient infrastructure, respectively (Bhan and Anand 2023). However, successful implementation depends on functional devolution of financial powers and coordination among various levels of government. Cities must align funding and authority to protect vulnerable informal workers effectively and produce economic output.

To address the problem of labor market fragmentation and understand the extent of the informal economy in the city region, cities should implement structured economic mapping systems (World Bank Group 2025a). Tools such as a City Economic Atlas, Migrant Labor Map, and Urban Informal Labor Dashboard can reveal the geographical distribution of informal, gig, and home-based workers, while highlighting labor market strengths

158 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

and weaknesses. Such information is particularly critical for MSMEs, which rely on local labor markets, informal supply chains, and proximity to workers and consumers, but often lack access to disaggregated and reliable data to inform location decisions, workforce and enterprise planning, and compliance pathways. These datasets become more effective when paired with job demand and skill forecasting tied to local industry clusters, such as textiles in Surat. State governments should support this effort through the creation of a unified Economic Observatory at the state level.

However, there is a need to move beyond employment policies to urban livelihood policies, missions, and city institutions that protect and formalize informal workers' access to space, services, social protection, and public contracts. This shift should also leverage MSME ecosystems, green job creation, and skilling as pathways for upward mobility. Further, it is crucial to embed informal workers' organizations in planning, implementation, and monitoring processes so that the substantial economic value they generate—often in dense informal settlements such as Dharavi—shapes, rather than is displaced by, urban economic development strategies.

Cities need dedicated municipal teams with labor specialists, social protection officers, and GIS experts to drive a robust livelihoods agenda, supported by budgets for migrant services, childcare, and gender inclusion (OECD 2020). State governments must decentralize responsibilities under the 74th CAA, offer financial incentive grants to cities meeting livelihoods and inclusion targets, and require updates to City Livelihood Plans every five years for ongoing monitoring of urban poverty and vulnerability. This approach ensures coordinated, data-driven efforts to support informal workers and reduce inequalities.

#### BOX 16 | Building MSME resilience in Surat's Growth Hubs

Surat's rise as a textile and industrial hub has been powered by thousands of MSMEs, yet these firms now operate under mounting climate risk. The wider Surat Economic Region faces recurrent flooding, cyclones, and sea-level-related hazards along the Tapi and coastal belt, threatening industrial estates, transport links, and power networks critical for MSMEs. The Economic Master Plan for the Surat Economic Region (G-Hub) responds by reorganizing and upgrading MSME production systems to cut environmental and climate risk and enhance their competitiveness. It proposes new and modernized industrial estates with common effluent treatment; shared utilities; and better internal roads, logistics, and connectivity, enabling MSMEs to relocate from congested, exposed inner-city clusters to planned, better-serviced sites.

Textile MSMEs in dyeing and printing currently operate in dense clusters with poor building design and extreme indoor heat and humidity, while a largely migrant workforce lives in infrastructure-poor neighborhoods with weak social protection. By combining estate upgrades with e-bus services, rental housing, childcare, schools, basic services, skills development, and cleaner technologies, the Growth Hubs vision creates conditions for a shift toward more climate-resilient, low-carbon MSME systems. Initiatives such as Resilient, Inclusive and Sustainable Enterprises (RISE) Surat can then be scaled and aligned within this regional framework so that investments in land, transport, housing, and utilities systematically strengthen MSME climate resilience.

Source: NITI Aayog 2024b; WRI India n.d.; Yadav 2025.

## Challenge 3

**Government initiatives aimed at establishing industrial clusters, SEZs, and corridors often resulted in the creation of isolated enclaves adjacent to major urban centers. These enclaves lack robust regional connections and have not succeeded in balancing broader regional growth with reducing inequality and improving sustainability.**

Industrial and economic policies such as SEZs, National Industrial Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs), and industrial corridors such as the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) are creating new greenfield economic settlements across India, which are emerging as industrial hubs with urban characteristics. SEZs are largely concentrated in industrialized districts and near large metropolitan areas in order to utilize already established amenities (Palit 2009; Kennedy and Rundell 2014; Jenkins et al. 2015). Out of 375 SEZs (as of December 1, 2017), 283 were located in the districts of million-plus cities (Tewari 2020).

Many of the approved SEZs are large enclaves, poorly linked to surrounding settlements, which reduces their potential for spillover benefits (Aggarwal 2010). As of 2017, over 20,000 hectares of land in SEZs in India remained unused (Sapra 2022), because planners misjudged how much land was needed, faced slow approval processes for government SEZs, and saw private developers holding on to land. As a result, policymakers changed their view of SEZs. They now see them not just as places for exports, but as integrated hubs for jobs and economic activity (Ministry of Commerce and Industry 2018). However, these hubs

should have good infrastructure, affordable housing nearby, and a supportive environment for businesses. China's Shenzhen Special Economic Zone provides an example of this new thinking. It is one of the largest SEZs in the world and resulted from a developmental approach where SEZ objectives are aligned with national development priorities and integrated into long-term urban planning frameworks (Wessendorp et al. 2020).

The GoI plans to craft a new SEZ law. This offers an opportunity to mandate spatial planning and integration of SEZs into long-term urban planning and governance frameworks in order to embed them more firmly in the regional economy and give them better access to human capital.

Unlike more isolated SEZ enclaves, industrial corridors aim to create industrial townships, which could potentially integrate new settlements with existing economic and urban centers (see Figure 36). The state takes the lead in planning and developing transport infrastructure, meaning that resident populations will enjoy better mobility and quality of life even if the corridors fail to attract industries (Tewari 2020). However, there is a governance gap for such projects because "industrial townships" are exempt from the 74th-CAA municipal framework, and they fall outside regular urban planning and service delivery (Anand et al. 2014). The greenfield components of the corridors are delegated to SPVs for governance.

## Recommendation 3

### Develop stronger links between industrial and economic policies and urbanization.

An NUP should seek convergence of place-based economic development models promoted through industrial and economic policies with mainstream urban development to catalyze investment in infrastructure within special projects and in their periphery and zones of influence, which extend into other urban areas.

The lack of large infrastructure-integrated serviced land often proves to be a deterrent for setting up industrial townships and areas. However, Tamil Nadu's experience shows how a state can invest in physical infrastructure ranging across roads, rail, ports, and communication infrastructure. Tamil Nadu's industrial policy emphasizes a mix of manufacturing- and services-led growth and addresses the spatial dimension of industrial development by creating serviced land banks with roads, water supply, and power. It also allocates land for promoting industrial parks and SEZs in peri-urban areas, providing infrastructure and facilities that attract industries and promote urbanization (Industries, Investment Promotion and Commerce Department 2024).

When agricultural land gets taken over by industries, skilling programs are needed to support the transition of surplus agricultural labor into industrial and service sectors. Industrial policies sometimes include incentives for employers to invest in the training and development of their workforce. States can implement schemes such as the Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Antyodaya Yojana (DAY) to provide skills training and expand its scope beyond STs to include newly created industrial settlements and CTs. In these industrial areas, skill development programs should focus on developing specific manufacturing-related skills to match the local demand for labor. Such land-use transitions can also raise concerns about the implications for agricultural production and food systems, particularly when conversion occurs in regions with high agricultural value. Managing these trade-offs requires coordinated land-use, agricultural, and workforce policies, so that urban and industrial expansion supports economic transformation without undermining long-term food security or rural livelihoods.

## Challenge 4

**A fragmented policy that frames migration solely as a labor issue rather than addressing it as a larger welfare problem excludes migrants in multiple ways in urban areas.**

India has over 450 million internal migrants (Rajan and Bhagat 2022). They make up a large percentage of the informal sector workforce in both rural and urban areas. However, these workers are among the most vulnerable, facing poor working conditions and limited access to social safety nets. Male migrants are mainly drawn to cities by opportunities for employment (ORGI 2011j). Women migrate mainly due to movement with family, or after marriage. According to the Census of 2011, while rural-to-rural migration remains dominant, its share is declining, while rural-to-urban and urban-to-urban migrations are on the rise.

Over the last two decades, transportation infrastructure and telecommunications advancements have dramatically improved connectivity, facilitating migration and rural-to-urban commuting. Improved roads, rail networks, and mobile communication have made it easier for individuals to relocate from rural areas to urban areas, where they hope to find work and improve their living conditions (Srivastava 2012).

Policy guidance on migration in India is fragmented, primarily addressing the labor rights of migrants in the informal sector without considering the interconnected issues of housing, infrastructure, and basic amenities. This lack of cohesion leads to increased informality in housing, inadequate rental protections, and exclusion from welfare benefits and urban safety nets. As a result, most migrant households struggle to find secure housing and remain outside formal urban planning and services, leaving them vulnerable in the long term (Srivastava 2020a). (see Table 18 for laws and policies governing labor and migration in India).

Universal entitlements focus on migrants through centrally sponsored schemes related to basic education, primary health care, early childhood care, and food security that are partly funded by the GoI (Naik 2023). However, migration governance depends on collaboration between the GoI and state governments on policy design and implementation (MoHUPA 2017a). State action includes two types of arrangements: a centralized scheme designed with states as implementing arms, or state-led scheme design and implementation (Naik 2023).

Analysis of data by scholars shows that in-migration correlates positively with urbanization level, per capita bank deposits, per capita net state domestic product, and per capita bank credit to industry (Das et al. 2012). Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, the top two states with the highest

interstate out-migrating population to urban areas (see Figures 37a and 37b) have low urbanization rates and high multidimensional poverty. Conversely, the top states, Maharashtra, Delhi, and Gujarat, with the highest interstate in-migrating population to urban areas have the high urbanization rates and low multidimensional poverty (see Figures 38a and 38b).

Many states struggle to coordinate their policies for managing migrant workers. Various government bodies, departments, and regulators often handle migrant worker regulations separately, which can create problems for workers trying to access their rights and benefits from state and federal programs.

- **Interstate migrants** face greater hardships. Regulations and administrative procedures exclude migrants from accessing legal rights, public services, and social protection programs accorded to residents (UNESCO 2013b).
- **Seasonal migrants** with low levels of education and skills are more vulnerable in urban areas. Often lacking proof of identity and residence, these migrants are excluded from social security (Panda and Mishra 2018).
- **Women migrants** are less likely to hold regular jobs and more likely to be self-employed. They are paid less than male migrants, and women and adolescent girls in informal jobs remain vulnerable to sexual harassment and abuse (UNESCO 2013a).
- **Migrant children** face learning difficulties based on differences in academic curricula and language (MoHUPA 2017b).

## Recommendation 4

**Articulate a governance structure for migration and interstate mobility that enables vertical and horizontal coordination between the GoI and state governments, ministries and departments, and individual states in order to handle migration as a broader developmental issue.**

To manage migration as a developmental issue, establish a clear governance structure that ensures vertical coordination from the GoI through state and city administrations, and horizontal collaboration across ministries (e.g., labor, housing, education, transportation) and states. Currently, data sharing and welfare alignment across states are weak, and within-state coordination of planning and service delivery is fragmented. Programs such as One Nation One Ration Card and Affordable Rental Housing Complexes have improved the access of migrants to welfare, while states such as Jharkhand, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha conducted skill mapping for returning migrants during the COVID-19 pandemic. Delhi and Maharashtra introduced targeted support such as mobile health support. However, many states lack integrated approaches combining housing, infrastructure, and social services. A GoI–state coordination platform, interstate migration councils, and shared data systems are needed to strengthen governance vertically and horizontally.

Migrant welfare suffers due to uneven implementation of social protection and poor portability of entitlements across states. Existing digital platforms (e.g., e-Shram) are fragmented, unevenly adopted, and often inaccessible to circular and seasonal migrants (Srivastava 2020b). A comprehensive NUP must mandate true portability of social protections—covering food, health care, childcare, and social security—along with grievance redressal, irrespective of migrants’ location or employer.

SMTs in India play a critical role in reducing rural poverty and serve as intermediaries for migrants before they move to large cities (Gibson et al. 2017). However, these towns face significant governance challenges due to limited authority over land use, housing, industry, and labor, which restricts their ability to plan effectively for migrants’ needs or provide essential services such as rental housing, childcare, and skills training. Additionally, coordination among state urban departments, labor ministries, industrial development agencies, and municipal administrations is often lacking, limiting urban governance capabilities (Athar et al. 2022). This leads many migrant households, especially women working informally, to live in substandard housing and unsafe neighborhoods and depend on informal subcontracting arrangements that restrict access to credit and social protection (World Bank Group 2025a). Better interdepartmental coordination at the state level, clear

delineation of responsibilities, and empowerment of local governments are essential to align planning, infrastructure, and services with the needs of migrants. Strengthening these towns could shift short-distance migration to commuting, easing pressure on big cities and improving the livelihoods of migrants.

Empowering SMTs to identify migrant-dense areas, adopting localized childcare models such as Surat’s Anganwadis,$^{5}$ and connecting skills training directly to local industries by conducting targeted assessments will enhance the safety, productivity, and integration of migrants. Coordinated efforts to study the needs of migrant youth and families will help these towns provide vocational training, hostel accommodation, reliable social services, and labor market alignment. Strengthening these towns can shift short-distance migration into commuting, easing the pressure on metros and improving migrant livelihoods. Overall, clear delineation of responsibilities, better interdepartmental cooperation, and holistic support at local levels are essential to secure India’s future labor force and promote equitable regional development.

## Challenge 5

### Urban poor children, adolescents, and youth face multidimensional deprivation that puts India's demographic dividend at risk.

India's demographic dividend—a period when the country has a disproportionately large working-age population (in India, this is considered to be 15–59 years) compared to dependents (over 60 years)—has long been considered a key driver of economic growth. In 2011, the median age was 24.92 years, projected to rise to 34.48 years by 2036 (MoHFW 2020). Despite declining fertility and growing longevity, this demographic advantage persists. It was estimated that whereas in 2020 the average age in India was 29 years, it was 40 years in the United States, 46 in Europe, and 47 in Japan (Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015). Thus, India's population remains significantly younger than the aging populations in other parts of the world, providing a comparably unique opportunity to harness the country's young workforce. However, without effective investments in nurturing healthy, educated, and skilled youth capable of contributing to the economy, this potential dividend risks becoming a liability.

Children, adolescents, and youth living in urban poverty face significant barriers that reduce their ability to thrive and contribute to inclusive development. According to National Family Health Survey (NFHS)-5 (2019–2021), 30–38 percent of children in urban India are undernourished. Early undernutrition, especially in the first 1,000 days of life, causes irreversible cognitive damage, but improving nutrition during this window can increase adult earnings by 5–50 percent and raise GDP by 4–11 percent (Global Panel on Agriculture and Food Systems for Nutrition 2016).

Despite programs such as Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and the National Health Mission (NHM), urban poor children suffer from persistent stunting and undernutrition. Urban health services often meet only 40 percent of required care—for example, Delhi's eight Primary Health Centres, with only basic outpatient care, immunization, and minor treatments, serve over 20 million residents with no Community Health Centres, which are higher-level bedded facilities with specialist services (Kumar and Saiyed 2019).

Data from UDISE+ 2024–25 (Ministry of Education 2025) show school dropout rates in India rising from about 0.3 percent at the primary level (ages 6–11) to 3.5 percent at the upper primary level (ages 11–14) and reaching 11.5 percent at the secondary school level (ages 14–18). Boys drop out more frequently than girls, with secondary-level dropout rates of 13.3 percent for boys versus 9.6 percent for girls (Ministry of Education 2025).

These dropout challenges are particularly acute in northern and central states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, where poverty, child labor, and poor infrastructure compound educational vulnerabilities (Ministry of Education 2025). Socioeconomic factors, especially among low-income migrant families, lead to declining retention and transition rates as children move through higher grades. Addressing financial, infrastructural, and social barriers at these educational junctures is essential to reduce dropout rates and build a skilled workforce that can drive India's economic growth.

Beyond education, poor urban residents face a stark service divide in housing, health care, education, transport, water, sanitation, energy, and social security. This multidimensional poverty disproportionately impacts children and youth. In low-income, low-urbanized states such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Jharkhand, India's growing working-age population faces a shortage of jobs, driving up NEET rates. These states also suffer from high multidimensional poverty and limited local opportunities. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, with especially young populations, see the highest rates of outward migration as discussed in the previous section.

Recent all-India data on NEET paint a worrying picture:

- In 2023, about 23.5 percent of Indian youth aged 15–24 were NEET, which is notably higher than the same percentages for comparable countries such as China (11.5 percent), Indonesia (21.3 percent), and Brazil (20.6 percent) (World Bank Group 2024b).
- As of 2021, the NEET rate for the total urban population was 27 percent (compared to 30 percent for rural), with considerably higher rates for urban women (38.3 percent) than for urban men (17.2 percent) (MoSPI 2021).
- There is considerable asymmetry between men and women: the number of women in NEET was almost five times that of their male counterparts (48.4 percent versus 9.8 percent) and accounted for around 95 percent of the total in 2022 (ILO 2024).
- Women who are "out of the labor force," that is, unemployed and also not in education and training, dominate the NEET population. This is because 90 percent of the women in NEET are involved in domestic and household work for their own households (ILO 2021).

This large NEET population highlights a critical mismatch between labor market needs and youth skills, resulting in unemployment, diminished economic output, and rising social exclusion.

172 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

The pronounced gender gap suppresses women's workforce participation, deepening economic inequality.

The National Youth Policy 2023–2032 addresses youth employability through education, skills development, entrepreneurship, and inclusivity. Although high-productivity sectors such as ICT, finance, and insurance grow in cities, informal labor dominates, and skill gaps persist in digital services, limiting the employment prospects of youth (Kaka et al. 2019).

## Recommendation 5

### **Invest in human capital by focusing on children and youth in urban poverty to avert a demographic disaster in low-urbanized states.**

Invest decisively in human capital by targeting children and youth in urban poverty, especially in low-urbanized states, to prevent a demographic and economic crisis. Cities must be designed to be inclusive and accessible, anchored by a human development framework that prioritizes vulnerable groups: migrants, children, youth in poverty, slum families, and informal workers. Ensuring seamless transitions from education to training and employment for all children regardless of caste, class, gender, or migration status requires tackling disparities in services, jobs, and social norms influencing parental attitudes, gender roles, and youth aspirations (ILO 2011).

Economic geography research on India indicates that two factors—post-secondary education and access to telecommunications—largely explain why high-density service clusters outperform other locations; when these factors are equalized across districts, the growth premium of dense clusters largely disappears (Desmet et al. 2013). This means that spatially targeted investments in human capital and digital infrastructure in medium-density cities and peri-urban regions are not only inclusion policies but key levers to unlock productivity and reduce the over-concentration of opportunity in a few metros. For children, adolescents, and young women in urban poverty, this translates into a need for city-region strategies that combine quality education, skills, and care infrastructure with the deliberate development of secondary employment centers and serviced land in locations where they live and can realistically access work, rather than expecting them to bridge growing spatial divides at their own cost.

Urban development strategies should complement the growth of digital and high-productivity sectors with investments in a care economy to foster equity. Addressing urban childhood malnutrition through improved ICDS coverage is critical, given its proven long-term economic benefits by enhancing cognitive development and future earnings (Hoddinott et al. 2013). City-specific youth action plans must link localized skills development with emerging

technology and digital economies, enabling youth—especially those from poor or migrant backgrounds—to shift from low-wage informal work to higher-wage sectors. ULGs, empowered with greater capacity and financial support, should coordinate the activities under the National Urban Livelihood Mission spanning health, education, skill building, and social protection to prevent exclusion and dropout.

National policies such as the National Youth Policy (2023–32) need strengthened coordination with industrial and urban policies. Successful models, such as Tamil Nadu's integrated approach combining industrial policy, welfare, and skilling, offer valuable lessons. Green job skill development warrants targeted attention, emphasizing the inclusion of women and marginalized groups with gender-responsive financing, incubation, and procurement support to tap India's green economy potential (OECD 2023; Cook and Elliott 2025). However, foundational education remains vital, because weak learning outcomes limit transitions to formal green or digital sectors (Dewan and Khan 2019).

SDG Target 4.4 requires countries to substantially increase the number of youth with relevant skills, including technical and vocational, for employment and entrepreneurship (Kundu 2020a). This would require national investment in youth to equip them with the necessary tools and knowledge to excel in a rapidly evolving digital landscape and other new jobs of the future.

This can be achieved if the NUP augments ULGs' resources, enabling them to create city-level interventions under a human development implementation agenda. ULGs should be equipped with the necessary tools to develop Youth Development Plans that identify how many children are out of school or at risk for dropping out of school—based on the prevalence of vulnerable populations and how many children are at NEET risk—and develop a pathway to jobs in the local labor market. The creation of Youth Development Plans will require that ULGs coordinate and cooperate with Health, ICDS, Education, Skills Development, and other departments in a single Urban Human Development Platform, so that the impacts of fragmented governance do not leave adolescents and youths behind and prevent them from falling into risks of exclusion, poor learning outcomes, and entry into precarious work. Implementing these tools is necessary for that purpose, otherwise the human capital commitments remain aspirational.

The NUP should also provide explicit instructions to cities regarding the scope of planning for youth infrastructure, such as including hostels for youth and female workers, safe study spaces for youths, vocational centers, hubs for digital access, and transitional housing or resting places for migrant adolescents who are entering the job force or

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 173

seeking work. These provisions will provide much-needed assistance and support for youths from low-income families and help them complete the transition from school to work, ensuring that they do not—due to insecure or unstable housing, lack of social protection or schooling—drop out from work or education before completing this transition.

ULGs and states should base youth skilling on local economic clusters to provide relevant, job-linked training rather than generic programs, enabling smoother

transitions out of informal work. They must develop gender-responsive green enterprise initiatives to overcome the structural barriers faced by women entrepreneurs. Complementarily, the NUP should mandate youth-friendly infrastructure in cities, including safe study spaces, hostels, vocational centers, and transitional housing, to support vulnerable youths’ school-to-work transitions and prevent dropout caused by insecure housing or lack of social protection.

## Challenge 6

**Low female labor force participation in urban areas and a lack of policy focus on care work compromise inclusive growth and broader development outcomes.**

Despite India's large-scale urbanization and the rhetoric of cities as engines of growth, female labor force participation (FLFP) is higher in rural areas (35.5 percent) than in urban areas (22 percent). Between 2017 and 2023, the FLFP rate for rural women nearly doubled, compared with just a marginal increase for urban women (see Figure 39).

India witnessed a sharp decline in the overall FLFP between the late 1980s and 2011, while the urban FLFP remained much lower than its rural counterpart and largely stagnated at around 18 percent (Klasen and Pieters 2015), even as the number of urban women in higher education increased from 46.5 percent in 2004–05 to 65.4 percent in 2017–18 (MoSPI 2019). Multiple, interwoven factors drive this persistent low female participation in urban India's workforce. Urban women bear a disproportionate share of household work and caregiving, including childcare and eldercare. Limited support infrastructure (such as affordable childcare, scarcity of safe transport) and flexible working hours limit women's ability to work, especially after marriage or childbirth. Exclusion from paid work stifles

women's contribution to economic growth and their ability to benefit from it. However, women's employment and earnings support their own and their children's well-being (Klasen and Pieters 2013). A mother's participation in the labor force increases the children's time spent in school and the level of education they achieve, in part because working women wield greater decision-making power in their households (Afridi et al. 2016).

For urban women, there is no positive correlation between the level of education and employment in urban areas. Urban economic growth has disproportionately created jobs in construction, last-mile delivery, or low-paying informal work, sectors dominated by men. Jobs suitable for or appealing to women, particularly educated women, have not grown proportionally. Although access to education has improved, many women either remain in education longer (delaying work entry) or drop out of the labor force after completing their studies due to a lack of desirable and suitable jobs (Lama 2021).
