175

On the other hand, less educated urban women, typically from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, are often forced to take lower-paid jobs, primarily in the informal sector, closer to their homes. However, women with higher education levels tend to be less willing to accept low-quality jobs or to travel long distances for work; however, employment opportunities are seldom available close to their homes. Interestingly, as women reach higher education levels, the percentage of those outside the labor force generally decreases (Ratho 2020). The lack of safe and stable transport in urban areas—in addition to social conservatism—poses a major challenge to women for undertaking paid work outside their localities, and contributes to low labor force participation of women in cities (Sircar 2019). A recent study (Jamba et al. 2025) of India’s first fare-free public transport (FFPT) scheme, launched in Delhi to enable women to travel for free in government buses, found increased bus use by Delhi’s women for short trips, enhancing their flexibility and autonomy. The scheme particularly benefited low-income women by saving them substantial household income (up to 8 percent). However, challenges such as overcrowding and noncompliance with seat reservation persist, pointing to the need to expand the bus fleet to address overcrowding and meet demand while designing bus schedules and routes to better align with women’s mobility needs.

Other factors prevent women from hailing public transport such as bus and metro rail. A study of metro access in three Indian cities found that women tend to use the metro for educational, shopping, and social trips more often, while men primarily use it for work-related trips (Mukherjee et al. 2023). Women tend to make shorter last-mile trips but pay more on average due to fare structures that do not align with their travel patterns, such as trip-chaining (combining multiple errands into one trip). Women are more averse to waiting for last-mile modes, especially in isolated or unsafe areas. Sexual harassment at bus stops and in crowded buses or trains is a significant deterrent. This often leads them to choose faster but more expensive options, such as auto-rickshaws, which offer flexibility in pick-up and drop-off points and help avoid crowded situations, increasing their travel costs.

The key legal provisions for women workers cover mainly formal employment, and include rules requiring separate toilets, creches, and canteens. A number of schemes aim to provide benefits to this demographic—see Table 19 for the central policies governing FLFP in urban India. The recent consolidation of India’s labor laws into four new labor codes—the Wages Code, Social Security Code, Industrial Relations Code, and Occupational Safety and Health Code—aims to simplify regulations and expand worker protections. However, a closer look reveals that these Codes still fail to adequately cover the majority of urban female workers in informal sectors such as home-based work,

micro-enterprises, domestic work, and the gig economy. Many protections, including minimum wage, safety, and social security benefits, are contingent on establishment-size thresholds that exclude most urban informal women workers. Consequently, the promised universal protections are effectively diluted, leaving these women vulnerable and underserved by the Codes. Despite positive measures, such as increased maternity leave and night shift allowances with safety protocols, implementation challenges and financial burdens on small enterprises hinder real access to benefits for women in precarious employment. Thus the Codes’ relevance for urban female informal workers remains limited, requiring targeted reforms and enforcement to truly advance their labor rights and protections (Mehrotra and Sharma 2025; Kulkarni 2025b).

## Recommendation 6

### An inclusive and equitable society must improve women’s workforce participation by investing in the care economy.

To boost women’s workforce participation—now at 41.7 percent in 2023–24, up from 23 percent in 2017–18 (News On Air 2025) but still trailing global peers—cities must invest in a coordinated care economy that values unpaid labor and eases the double burden of paid work and domestic duties. Fragmented policies, focused on formal sectors and siloed across ministries, overlook informal women workers in home-based, gig, domestic, and micro-enterprise roles. It is recommended that the NUP mandate that cities map women-dominated value chains (e.g., garments, food processing, beauty services), integrate them into economic planning, and provide safe workspaces, common facility centers, micro-credit, and formal market linkages to break invisible subcontracting traps (Behal 2023).

Complementing this measure with ILO’s “Decent Work Agenda” principles can be a good starting point for framing the principles of a care economy, not only recognizing unpaid care work but reducing drudgery, redistributing care work responsibilities between women and men, remunerating care workers, and representing their concerns. In addition, build on lessons from good practices implemented in countries such as Colombia, which set up an Intersectoral Commission to establish the creation of two statistical operations: the National Time-Use Survey (ENUT) and the Care Economy Satellite Account (CSEC) to establish a data-driven approach to Promoting Women’s Economic Empowerment and Investing in the Care Economy.

The NUP must also enforce labor codes at the city level—overcoming establishment-size thresholds—to extend wages, safety, and social security to informal women workers, while facilitating a well-distributed network of support infrastructure such as childcare—especially near industrial clusters, home-based production hubs, and neighborhoods where migrants reside—women-friendly transportation planning (scheduled routes, lighting, last-mile connectivity), and flexible home-based options. A 2011 ILO study found that 34 percent of women in rural India and about 28 percent of those in urban India would be willing to accept work if they could do it at home (Chaudhary and Verick 2014). Among these women, in both rural and urban areas, tailoring was the most preferred work, and about 95 percent preferred regular work. About 74 percent of women in rural areas and about 70 percent of those in urban areas preferred “part-time” work regularly, while 21 percent in rural areas and 25 percent in urban areas wanted regular “full-time” work.

Empower ULGs to customize Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-NULM (DAY-NULM) training courses to local industries rather than offering generic courses such as sewing, linking such training to jobs for female gig workers, migrant women, and poor women (Chatterji 2020). Expand urban wage schemes such as MUKTA and Ayyankali Urban Employment Guarantee Scheme, which build skills via public works and empower women’s SHGs as project managers, boosting income, capacity, and governance roles (see Box 17).

![img-30.jpeg](img-30.jpeg)

**BOX 17 | Urban wage programs for unemployed workers: The MUKTA scheme in Odisha and mainstreaming urban greening as a productive livelihood option through the Ayyankali scheme in Kerala**

**The Mukhya Mantri Karma Tatpara Abhiyan (MUKTA) scheme:** The onset of COVID-19 upended city life across the world. In the state of Odisha, India, lockdowns imposed during the pandemic created an acute unemployment and poverty crisis among the urban poor. The Government of Odisha created an Urban Wage Employment Initiative called the MUKTA scheme. This scheme works with existing civil society groups and adapts public-sector procurement processes to rapidly create mass jobs through an infrastructure program for the urban poor, informal workers, and migrant laborers to provide rapid relief to urban poor workers whose livelihoods were disrupted by the crisis. To date, workers across Odisha’s 114 cities have been employed to implement 22,500 climate-sensitive building projects including drain desilting, green cover, rainwater harvesting, community centers, sanitation activities, and public space development. In a departure from the traditional process of tendering public works, local authorities were guided by Odisha’s Housing and Urban Development Department to work directly with community groups, slum dwellers associations, and women’s self-help groups to deliver construction projects in local communities.$^{a}$

**Municipal greening and productive livelihood in Kochi, Kerala:** The Kochi Municipal Corporation has been planting native trees across the municipal area through a Kawaki initiative as part of the city’s climate action. Kochi city has effectively strategized a partnership with the Local Self Government Department (LSGD) of Kerala State—Ayyankali Scheme—to employ non-skilled women labourers to maintain the greening sites. Maintenance of green spaces became a viable and productive livelihood option for poor unskilled women in Kochi.$^{b}$

Source: a. WRI Ross Center Prize for Cities 2025. b. Sekhar 2023.

CHAPTER 9.

# Environmental Sustainability

The chapter explores how cities can manage environmental degradation, pollution, and water depletion, with particular attention to transitional peri-urban areas that grow rapidly under rural administration with minimal planning oversight. Key challenges include the heavy environmental burdens generated by unregulated urbanization in these zones, worsening urban air quality and the financing gaps in addressing it, and unsustainable water management practices threatening both water security and quality. The chapter pairs these challenges with targeted policy recommendations.

The booming urban population and rapid urban expansion have led to environmental challenges such as reduced biodiversity; growing air, water, and land pollution; and scarcity of water resources. A key challenge to protecting India's natural resources is the prevalent trend of sprawling patterns of urban expansion, which puts severe pressure on various fronts. Urban infrastructure struggles to keep up with outward spatial expansion and the demands of a growing population, leading to gaps in basic service and infrastructure (see Figure 40). By analyzing data from villages in the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region (BMR) and examining how access to utilities changes with increasing distance from the Bengaluru Municipal Corporation (i.e., Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike [BBMP]), we found that utility provision declines as one moves away from the city center, highlighting the fragmented regional benefits of urbanization. The percentage of households with PSSs drops significantly, and although private on-site systems, such as septic tanks, initially help mitigate this decrease, their effectiveness falls off beyond a certain distance.

The availability of closed wastewater drainage systems falls sharply just beyond the urban core and then stabilizes, indicating that these services are accessible primarily within a short distance from the city. This trend emphasizes the need for interventions to address spatial inequalities and ensure that all areas benefit from urbanization.

Revisions of municipal boundaries and statutory plans are often delayed. The result is that settlement patterns densify and spread long before they are formally recognized as “urban,” leaving new neighborhoods outside the reach of planned water, sanitation, transport, and drainage networks. Outward expansion from the city core increases average trip length and, consequently, carbon emissions (Pandit 2015). The ecosystems in areas where the city expands are often severely compromised, because many landfill sites are located outside city boundaries, and local governments outside municipal limits lack mandates for waste management. The result is damage to the environment and destruction of natural resources.

181

With the policy push to relocate industries outside city limits, villages outside metropolitan cities have seen significant growth in employment in manufacturing, real estate, transport, storage, and communication services (Vishwanath et al. 2013). Relocating industries from city cores to fast-growing villages and CTs tends to shift, rather than resolve, environmental pressures, creating new and often less regulated hotspots of degradation in these transitional spaces. These areas usually have weaker environmental oversight and limited infrastructure; as a result, industrial risks intersect with existing rural vulnerabilities, and new nonfarm employment patterns emerge.

This report, in Chapter 5, has advocated for compact and well-connected cities. In this chapter, the focus is on growth while simultaneously identifying and safeguarding natural environments in peri-urban spaces and transitional urban areas and taking a regional and/or metropolitan approach to environmental planning and governance. The recommendations in this chapter should be read alongside

the recommendations in Chapter 5, especially the ones requiring rationalization of planning boundaries, leveraging DPCs and MPCs for transitional area planning, and stronger data sharing. They must also be read alongside Chapter 10. The recommendations, while primarily focused on improving environmental governance and processes, also contribute to long-term climate change mitigation and adaptation.

**Policy landscape.** Indian environmental law and policy provide a relatively dense formal framework comprising a suite of laws and missions addressing water, air, forests, biodiversity, and climate. MoEFCC is the central ministry that oversees all matters relating to the environment. The CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) are authorized under the environmental acts to monitor and regulate air, water, and soil quality. See Table 20 for the national policy landscape of environment protection and pollution prevention.

However, research on peri-urban land-use change around Indian cities concludes that the current policies are poorly equipped to address sprawling, fragmented, and privately driven development. Systematic reviews of peri-urban governance highlight three recurring weaknesses (Follmann et al. 2018; Patel et al. 2025; Salem et al. 2025): unclear jurisdictional responsibility at the urban–rural interface; limited integration of land-use planning with environmental regulation; and a strong bias toward core cities rather than peripheral settlements.

Cities also routinely violate their master plans, and urban extensions infringe on protected green zones and eco-sensitive areas outside municipal limits (see Figures 41A and 41B). India also has a record of diluting environmental laws and notifications to ease developmental activities. For instance, the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification (1991) has been amended 34 times in 27 years, making it the most amended law in India’s history. In the latest amendment of 2018, the sensitive coastal zone has been severely deregulated, allowing a wide variety of construction, tourism, and reclamation activities, without any studies to understand the impact of increased developmental activities on marine life and coastal communities (Kukreti 2019).

The need of the hour is a coherent national-level agenda for protecting the environment, focusing on all scales of cities and transitional urban and peri-urban areas. Although many of the challenges relate to topics that are state governments’ responsibilities, a national agenda can help coalesce and catalyze action on many fronts by giving states, cities, and RLGs tools and blueprints to enable sustainable urban development.

## Challenges and Recommendations

### Challenge 1

**Unplanned, unmanaged, and unregulated urbanization in peri-urban and transitional areas under rural administration produces significant environmental burdens.**

Peri-urban settlements have become common destinations for industry, warehousing, and solid waste dumping because environmental regulations and zoning controls are generally weaker beyond municipal limits, and shifting activities to Gram Panchayat areas reduces both land and compliance costs. The case of Barjora (Box 18) illustrates how rapid industrialization in a CT, combined with a rural governance structure lacking urban service functions such as SWM, generates severe air, water, and waste burdens that local authorities are unable to address effectively. Large cities also locate landfills and quarry pits outside their boundaries, transferring pollution and health risks to neighboring villages that lack the legal authority and technical capacity to regulate these facilities. Large cities such as Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru dump a significant proportion of waste generated at the edge of the city (see Figure 42) in areas that were once distant suburbs, such as Deonar, Bhalswa, and Mavallipura (Goswami and Basak 2021). Similar instances have been reported in other parts of the country: for example, Visakhapatnam’s dumping yard at Kapuluppada is located 25 km from the city, and Gorakhpur dumps its waste in peri-urban villages such as Mahewa (Mani and Wajih 2021).

Market pressures for cheaper land and housing, combined with highways, industrial corridors, and logistics infrastructure, are pushing firms and households to regions beyond municipal boundaries, where land values are lower and regulations looser. This is producing continuous built-up corridors and suburban–peri-urban clusters that are economically integrated with city regions yet formally remain “rural,” complicating planning, taxation, and environmental oversight. For example, a WRI India study shows that between 2000 and 2015, the built-up area in 10 Indian cities grew by approximately half in the core (0–20 km) but more than doubled in the periphery (20–50 km), underscoring the pace of outward, often unregulated, growth (Goswami et al. 2023).

This pattern of industrial siting, informal development, and waste infrastructure redistributes environmental risks outward, relying on the appropriation of land and water from peri-urban and rural hinterlands, where resource-dependent communities have limited power to contest city–region interests. Because these impacts fall outside formal city boundaries, they sit in administrative gray zones

### BOX 18 | Barjora: The burdens of industrial development in Census Towns

Barjora was historically a small village surrounded by dense forests in West Bengal. In 2001, it became a Census Town and has retained that status since. The construction of a barrage road on the River Damodar in 1959 connected Barjora to Durgapur and Asansol, and a single-lane state highway improved the connection to the district headquarters of Bankura. The town experienced a surge in industrial activity, led by multinational companies, particularly after 2000. Coal mines and ferro industries were set up, attracted by cheap land, low production costs, and uninterrupted power supply. The most important incentive was Barjora's strategic location: it was accessible from the Durgapur-Asansol Industrial Area, but far from the oversight and control of the West Bengal Pollution Control Board. The industrial activity has since spilled over to surrounding villages in every direction along the main road connecting them to the nearby larger cities, impacting local infrastructure and services. The heavy industrial consumption of water has caused a severe water shortage, depleting supplies needed for farming and domestic use. Most households have a personal well or a deep tube well, because the water supplied by the panchayat is not sufficient. The groundwater dries up in summer, forcing residents to depend on water tankers. Industrial activity has also led to increased air pollution. Improper solid waste management is another pressing concern. Urbanization has led to an increased generation of waste, but the panchayat does not have sufficient capacity for proper waste management. Barjora's case exemplifies the kind of development occurring in Census Towns, where governance structures remain rural, funding and oversight are minimal, and there is no coordination between local bodies and environmental agencies.

Source: Samanta 2017.

where the responsibility for mitigation and regulation is ambiguous (Mitra et al. 2017).

Peri-urban landscapes experience rapid land degradation through the conversion of agricultural fields, sand mining, construction debris dumping, and waste disposal, often on village commons that hold high ecological and livelihood value for rural households (Mani and Wajih 2021). Chapter 5 discusses how common lands, particularly in rural areas, are increasingly being used for urban purposes, putting these lands and the communities dependent on them at risk. This poses environmental risks, because common lands hold immense ecological, economic, and sociocultural value, contributing on average 12–23 percent to rural household incomes in India. They play a role in crucial ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration; regulation of temperature, nutrient runoff, rainfall, and water flows; and biodiversity conservation (ElDidi et al. 2023). Chapter 6 discusses the relocation of landfills to fringe areas and the implications of inadequate waste management systems for land and water pollution.

Unplanned urban expansion and land-use change also impact soil health and fertility. Global and Indian studies on peri-urban and rural areas describe how increasing landscape fragmentation is leading to disrupted soil ecosystems, including shifts in soil diversity and bacterial composition. Changes in land use, reduction in forest cover, and growth of impervious surfaces have been directly linked to soil health (Li et al. 2023). Industrialization and rampant waste disposal have also led to a larger quantum of toxic contaminants, heavy metals, and microplastics in peri-urban soils (Ahogle et al. 2023). Not only does this impact the soil's ecosystem function—for example, nutrient cycling and water retention—but it also has effects on human health, food systems, and agricultural productivity (Herrmann et al. 2020). For instance, a study in Delhi showed heavy metal contamination of soil and irrigation water, exceeding the safety limits for vegetables such as okra, cauliflower, and spinach (Bhatia et al. 2015). Another study in Cooch Behar, West Bengal, revealed high microplastic levels in soil (Sarkar et al. 2022), suggesting that even relatively small towns—not only megacities—are now showing measurable microplastic pollution in their soils, likely linked to poor SWM, plastic use, and dumping. Together, the two studies indicate a spatial pattern (both big metros and small towns) and a contaminant pattern (heavy metals and microplastics) of rising soil and water pollution in urban and peri-urban food and living environments.

Similarly, groundwater systems in peri-urban India face multiple concurrent pressures, including contamination from surface-based activities and depletion from overextraction. Industrial effluents discharged into open drains further degrade groundwater quality, particularly in clusters located just outside municipal oversight.

A study in Karhera, a former agricultural village between New Delhi and Ghaziabad, found that increasing water demand from newly established high-rise apartments and malls had lowered groundwater levels, resulting in insufficient supply from tube wells. Alongside large-scale industrial activity in the area, it has also led to surface water pollution and impacted the agricultural practice in the region (Waldman et al. 2017). Lower water tables have also been observed in peri-urban areas, where green cover is rapidly being taken over by impervious surfaces (Mitra et al. 2017). The shrinkage of critical blue–green spaces, which often served as ecological buffers for nearby cities and rural areas, further impedes climate resilience in these already fraught landscapes.

Environmental issues such as water scarcity or land-use conflicts may be localized challenges but are symptoms of broader pressures emanating from regional industrial strategies or global supply-chain imperatives. For example, the growth of IT corridors and industrial corridors such as the Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC) represents a case of metropolitan ambition conflicting with environmental impacts and social realities. It creates tensions with surrounding peri-urban areas because it affects local water systems, biodiversity, and agriculture, and creates social displacement (see Box 19). Further, poor spatial planning in core and peri-urban areas is shrinking natural blue–green resources and productive or agricultural land. This further diminishes the urban resilience capacity that peri-urban areas naturally offer (Narain, Khan et al. 2013).

Inadequate governance mechanisms compound the effect of fragmented, low-density expansions that strain natural systems, given that peri-urban areas typically come under rural governments that lack environmental mandates, technical capacity, and financial resources (Narain, Anand et al. 2013). See Box 19 for a case study on how lack of environmental governance causes ecological damage in peri-urban villages. Current governmental responses to integrating peri-urban areas into urban governance structures in India remain largely reactive, fragmented, and state-specific, often responding only after conflicts, disasters, or service breakdowns become visible. Empirical work on the peri-urban interface describes how overlapping mandates between panchayats, ULGs, and parastatal agencies, combined with low political priority, institutional inertia, and contested land interests, delay timely reclassification of urbanizing villages as municipalized urban areas and hamper their integration into regional spatial planning (see the case study of Bhiwandi notified area, discussed in Chapter 5). As a result, many transitional settlements fall into administrative gray zones where neither rural nor urban institutions take full responsibility for planning, environmental management, and infrastructure investment (Narain et al. 2014; Lakshmisha et al. 2016; Narain, Anand et al. 2013).

#### BOX 19 | The Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC) and its impact on the peri-urban environment

CBIC is a flagship project that links the two cities through a high-speed freight corridor and associated industrial zones as a catalyst for regional development. It is a mega project that is expected to generate economic opportunities through improved connectivity and transform agricultural lands into industrial hubs. Manufacturing industries and rapid urbanization in the region are expected to disrupt ecosystems, creating stress on natural resources while reducing access to traditional livelihoods for local populations. Local communities, which are excluded from the decision-making processes, face challenges related to compensation, rehabilitation, and loss of access to common resources. The following environmental and social impacts are noted:

- Large-scale land acquisitions for industrial parks have taken away green cover, water resources, and agricultural biodiversity.
- Groundwater depletion has been exacerbated by industrial water usage. Overextraction of groundwater for urban and industrial uses has led to declining water tables, saltwater intrusion, and reduced water quality. Farmers dependent on groundwater for irrigation are increasingly unable to sustain agricultural activities, leading to economic distress and migration.
- Farmers displaced by land acquisitions face loss of traditional livelihoods, inadequate compensation, and social dislocation.
- Migrant workers, who form the bulk of the labor force in industrial hubs, endure precarious living and working conditions.

Source: Woiwode et al. 2024.

# Recommendation 1

**Take a regional approach to environmental governance and planning to strengthen environmental safeguards in peri-urban and transitional areas and restrict the negative externalities of urbanization, such as groundwater depletion, land and soil pollution, and loss of ecologically valuable common lands.**

A national urbanization strategy must prioritize a metropolitan or regional approach to environmental governance to curb degradation in peri-urban and transitional areas.

Stronger national guidance on peri-urban integration, state-level regulatory and planning reforms, and empowered local and community institutions are all required to address land, water, waste, and governance challenges in these administrative gray zones. As previous chapters, specifically Chapter 2, have pointed out, peri-urban areas need to be explicitly recognized in national and state policy (definitions, data, and planning mandates), and planning areas need to be extended to cover functional city regions where these areas occur.

Environmental regulation and monitoring should be tightened in rural and fringe jurisdictions where industrial and waste facilities are relocating and accompanied by clear liability and grievance mechanisms. In addition, dedicated institutional and financing arrangements for peri-urban infrastructure, blue-green buffers, and commons protection should be created with district- and metropolitan-scale coordination.

The strategy should prioritize preservation of peri-urban ecosystems and protect and enhance blue-green infrastructure as cities expand. The first step should be to take stock of green areas outside forests and ecologically sensitive areas, especially in transitional and peri-urban areas, through GIS-based mapping. Documenting biodiversity in these areas can help support the development of necessary conservation programs through tools such as People's Biodiversity Registers. A planning category could also be created in the Town and Country Planning Act that allows cities and states to mark out peri-urban ecosystems and devise frameworks for protecting them. Urban forestry projects—such as those encouraged by the Nagar Van Yojana—can help create and maintain green infrastructure in the peri-urban areas that are most vulnerable to urban expansion. Developing guidance for planning in transitional urban areas will be key to better environmental governance. Transitional spaces—where large villages, peri-urban areas, and CTs are expanding—need a strategy to address the negative externalities of urban sprawl. Planners responsible for these transitional zones can use the RADPFI guidelines as a starting point, which recommend that 8–10 percent of land use in villages be reserved for environmental purposes. This is critical because unregulated sprawl driven by market imperatives will otherwise make peri-urban and transitional spaces unlivable.

## Challenge 2

**Indian cities are among the most polluted in the world, but there is a lack of uniformity in the criteria for sector-based mitigation actions across clean air action plans. Funding for particulate matter (PM) reduction has been heavily skewed toward PM10 reduction, leaving the deadlier PM2.5 largely unaddressed. Moreover, a city-centric approach impedes coordination at an airshed or regional scale.**

Air pollution levels in India are among the highest in the world (World Bank 2024). Approximately 1.4 billion people in India are exposed to unhealthy levels of ambient PM2.5—the most harmful pollutant—emanating from multiple sources (Pun et al. 2017; Alexeeff et al. 2021). Emerging studies have also linked PM2.5 exposure to pregnancy loss (Xue et al. 2021) and reduced life expectancy (Apte et al. 2018). In fact, in 2021, India saw the largest air-pollution-related deaths among children under five and accounted for half of global deaths related to ozone pollution (Health Effects Institute 2024).

In early 2019, MOEFCC launched the NCAP, requiring states and cities to reduce concentrations of harmful PM, particularly PM2.5 and PM10 (Chowdhury and Kumari 2024). FC-15, in its October 2020 report, allocated an additional INR 44 billion ($600 million) for curbing air pollution and identified 42 large cities or UAs, including 34 already identified as non-attainment cities under the NCAP. Currently, 131 cities jointly come under India’s air quality management program (Chowdhury and Kumari 2024). As of 2024, 24 states and Union Territories had prepared State Action Plans, and all 131 cities had developed City Action Plans (CAPs), as required under the program (Chowdhury and Kumari 2024).

However, there are inconsistencies in the methods used to evaluate clean air performance across these two programs as well as across the years. Table 21 summarizes the methods used for the years 2020–21 and 2021–22. As the table illustrates, the evaluation criteria are different for the two years, FC-15 cities have an additional criterion for both years, and the baseline years differ. Complicating this further, an additional evaluation layer was added in 2022 in the form of the Swachh Vayu Survekshan, which ranks cities based on clean air actions taken under CAPs. The varying parameters have led to the same cities being ranked differently under different systems.

A second key challenge is the lack of state-of-the-art monitoring infrastructure and inadequate understanding of pollution sources, which requires urgent attention. Under the National Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP), India has more manual monitoring stations than continuous ambient air quality monitoring (CAAQM) stations, the type capable of generating real-time data to capture PM2.5 levels. Moreover, only 36 cities (27.69 percent) had conducted source apportionment studies as on August 2025 (PRANA n.d.). Without these studies, cities lack a comprehensive understanding of the causes of air pollution. This creates two distinct challenges:

- The lack of pollution source analysis has partly resulted in a disproportionate policy focus on PM10 reduction over PM2.5 reduction. Although NCAP’s stated objectives include reductions in both PM10 and PM2.5, in practice, most action has been limited to dust management and improvement of ambient air quality. As much as 64 percent of the total NCAP funds has gone to projects such as road paving and widening, pothole repair, water sprinkling, and the use

190 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

of mechanical sweepers, with much less going to actions to reduce PM2.5 pollution: controlling biomass burning (14.51 percent), vehicular pollution (12.63 percent), and industrial pollution (0.61 percent) (Chowdhury and Kumari 2024).

The second challenge is an incomplete understanding of cross-boundary air pollution. For instance, a 2019 study found that about 50 percent of PM2.5 in Delhi's ambient air comes from outside, half from Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. Similarly, in Punjab, it was found that 60 percent of PM2.5 in ambient air comes from outside the state, including neighboring countries (Purohit et al. 2019). A more recent study by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (Manojkumar and Raj 2026) showed that around 65 percent of Delhi's PM2.5 burden is attributed to inflow from outside the city, mainly other NCR districts and neighboring states, with only 35 percent from local sources; winter data confirm that transported pollution outweighs in-city emissions. Both studies underline that Delhi cannot "clean its air alone" and that a large share of PM2.5 is regional or transboundary in origin, supporting the case for airshed-level control strategies rather than city-only measures.

In addition, India's air quality management program demonstrates metropolitan bias in its funding, at the expense of rural and peri-urban areas. Of the total INR 197.11 billion earmarked for FY 2019–20 to 2025–26, only 16 percent (INR 31.72 billion) has been allocated to 82 cities under the NCAP and about 84 percent (INR 165.39 billion) to the million-plus cities under the FC-15 grant (Chowdhury and Kumari 2024).

## Recommendation 2

MoEFCC and the Ministry of Finance jointly need to establish uniform criteria for air quality performance evaluation. MoEFCC needs to conduct robust source apportionment studies, leveraging data to link clean air action with public health. More coordination is needed across entire regions or “airsheds,” where air circulates and pollutants potentially impact the entire area.

Improving air-quality-monitoring infrastructure will aid efforts to develop an airshed policy (Guttikunda et al. 2023), which is crucial to addressing the misconception that air pollution is a localized problem. The World Bank defines an airshed as a “region that shares a common flow of air, which may become uniformly polluted and stagnant” (World Bank 2024). An airshed approach helps address environmental externalities originating from outside city limits.

Moreover, it provides an opportunity to address pollution in small towns, suburbs, and rural areas, which may not have adequate capacity and infrastructure for air management. An airshed policy could allow small cities and towns to benefit from shared infrastructure for waste management, transport, and so on, that services clusters rather than individual cities.

Developing detailed emissions inventories, monitoring, and modeling to estimate the dispersion and transportation of pollutants can help with the accurate determination of airsheds (Ghosh et al. 2023). Once this is done, India can notify airsheds through existing policy provisions, such as Section 19 of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, which allows delineation of “air pollution control areas” (Ghosh et al. 2023).

Experience with previous efforts at regional pollution management in India (see Box 20) shows that implementation is often lax, and so developing a robust governance framework for airshed management is a major anticipated challenge. Therefore, creating an institutional body to oversee governance in each identified airshed and clearly delineating its duties, powers, and jurisdiction are crucial. Some experts recommend that the new body assume the rulemaking and standard-setting role, limiting implementation powers to states and ULGs. This would allow for coordinated airshed planning without the need to create new capacities for implementation and enforcement (Ghosh et al. 2023). Alternatively, the powers and provisions under existing regional bodies, where they already exist, can be strengthened. To avoid further jurisdictional conflict, the airshed management body could be given overriding powers over ULGs and states in all matters pertaining to air quality across the airshed region.

## BOX 20 | Efforts toward regional pollution management

In November 2024, the Uttar Pradesh cabinet cleared its Clean Air Project, to be funded by the World Bank, paving the way for what is being proposed as India’s first airshed project.$^{a}$

The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) also offers a working model for the National Capital Region (NCR) and adjoining areas, coordinating air quality efforts in the NCR region of Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan.$^{b}$

Prior to this, the Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ) Authority was set up in 1999 through a notification under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The Authority, which has jurisdiction over Agra Division in Uttar Pradesh and Bharatpur Division in Rajasthan, is responsible for ensuring compliance with vehicular emissions and fuel quality standards in the region adjoining the Taj Mahal. However, data are not available on administrative steps taken by the Authority for implementation.$^{c}$

## Challenge 3

**Poorly planned cities and urban expansion are undermining groundwater, degrading water bodies, and weakening flood resilience, while fragmented governance and lagging reforms block integrated, demand-side, city-region water management.**

Weak spatial planning and business-as-usual infrastructure choices are locking Indian cities into a high-risk water trajectory. Urban growth continues to degrade groundwater, surface water, and flood resilience because institutions, regulations, and investments have not been realigned with hydrological realities or with demand-side management. In urban and urbanizing areas, heavy reliance on groundwater (Chandra and Janakiraman 2022) has led to drained aquifers and lowered water tables, and covering land with concrete makes it harder for groundwater to recharge (Goswami et al. 2023). Indeed, all increases in spatial extents of built-up area, whether planned or unplanned, managed or unmanaged, change existing natural spaces and impact surface and sub-surface hydrological flows (Wu et al. 2019; Blum et al. 2020). The 2023 census of all the water bodies in the country, totaling some 2.4 million (PIB 2023b), found that of the 70,000 water bodies classified as urban, a significant portion were reported as “not in use,” for various reasons such as drying up, siltation, or construction (Ministry of Jal Shakti 2023).

Pollution is another critical problem, affecting groundwater, rivers, and lakes. Water bodies have become severely polluted due to the indiscriminate discharge of industrial effluents, untreated sewage, and municipal waste (Jadeja et al. 2022). Pollution control failures are fundamentally governance failures. Industrial effluents, untreated sewage,

and solid waste continue to enter rivers and lakes because most cities lack universal sewerage coverage, adequate treatment capacity, and credible enforcement. Monitoring systems remain episodic and compliance driven rather than risk based and continuous, limiting regulators’ ability to detect peak loads, prosecute polluters, or target investments where they matter most. Although the number of sites monitored has increased, the methods and processes used remain problematic (Lele et al. 2021). For instance, samples are often collected only from polluted sites, often as “grab samples”: taken at a fixed time once in three or four months. The absence of continuous monitoring hinders accuracy. For instance, continuous monitoring of Bengaluru’s Vrishabhavathi river found much higher peak levels of pollution in the night and early morning than during the day (Jamwal et al. 2022). The creation of online, real-time monitoring systems, as prescribed by a 2017 Supreme Court judgment, continues to lag (Harshvardhan 2024a).

Resource and capacity gaps compound these problems, especially for SMTs. A recent directive from the National Green Tribunal to establish uniform standards for water pollution has caused a great deal of confusion, mainly because these norms would require enormous financial resources to implement, especially for smaller cities (Harshvardhan 2024b). Uniform standards and ambitious mandates are being issued without commensurate fiscal transfers, technical assistance, or phased implementation pathways, creating confusion and weak compliance rather than genuine improvements in water quality.

![img-37.jpeg](img-37.jpeg)

Urban flood risk illustrates how governance undermines resilience. Land-use decisions routinely place dense development in low-lying recharge and drainage zones, while stormwater networks remain under-designed, poorly maintained, and disconnected from broader catchment management. Encroachment on lakes, tanks, and wetlands—often enabled by institutional silos and weak enforcement—removes critical buffer capacity just as climate change intensifies rainfall extremes. Stormwater infrastructure in most cities is incomplete, old, not designed for the severe events experienced today, and inadequately maintained, which results in suboptimal performance, leaving urban areas more vulnerable to flooding (Goswami et al. 2023).

WRI analysis suggests that India faces extreme water stress every year (World Resources Institute 2025). Although water is a state subject, it is successive central governments that have enacted policies and schemes to tackle the water management issues Indian cities face. The National Water Policy sought to streamline water resource management, but it relied heavily on technocratic, supply-based approaches that aimed to increase water supply through the control of natural systems. However, the promise of endlessly increasing water supply creates the risk of overextraction and ecological harm. By contrast, demand management strategies emphasize optimizing the use of available water, reuse of wastewater, and efficiency improvements. A proposed amendment to the National Water Policy, drafted in 2020, could signal this shift. It prioritizes Integrated Water Resources Management (Shah 2021), which reduces the demand load by understanding and responding to water systems' dynamic and interconnected nature. However, adoption of this amendment has been delayed, resulting in a missed opportunity to catalyze change (Ghosh 2024).

Central schemes that address urban water management, including Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), Jal Jeevan Mission, and Jal Shakti Abhiyan, operate within sectoral and rural–urban silos. Although AMRUT plays an important role in urban water systems and the Jal Jeevan Mission does so for rural water systems, peri-urban and semi-rural areas that bear the brunt of urban expansion fall between mandates, revealing the need for clearer jurisdictional responsibilities, streamlined funding channels, and explicit governance arrangements for managing water across the full city-region continuum.

## Recommendation 3

**To respond to India's urban water and flood risks, policy must move from piecemeal projects to integrated, closed-loop water governance at the city-region scale. This requires aligning spatial planning, regulation, financing, and schemes with conserving and reusing water, groundwater monitoring, and protecting hydrological systems as core infrastructure.**

First, the GoI and state governments should incentivize closed-loop urban water systems by issuing clear, practical directives and standards for wastewater reuse, stormwater capture, conjunctive use of surface and groundwater, and systematic monitoring of groundwater quantity and quality, backed by financing and regulatory reforms. Strengthening and updating the National Water Policy (Shah 2021), with an explicit emphasis on demand management and Integrated Water Resources Management, is critical to move away from supply-driven, infrastructure-heavy responses toward efficiency, reuse, and ecosystem protection. This must be accompanied by amendments to the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act and related regulations to tighten enforcement, mandate reuse and resource recovery where feasible, and enable regulators to act across urban, peri-urban, and rural jurisdictions. At the same time, the national groundwater framework—anchored in the Central Ground Water Board and the Model Groundwater Bill, 2017—needs to be strengthened to close gaps in data, regulation, and accountability that currently hinder sustainable management of India's heavily exploited aquifers.

Second, urban spatial planning instruments need to be retooled as water governance tools, not just land allocation devices. Master plans should systematically integrate water security and flood resilience by requiring environmental and hydrological assessments for new development; using stormwater runoff simulations to guide densities and layouts; designating low-impact development (LID) and blue-green infrastructure (BGI) zones; and using incentives (e.g., FAR bonuses, fee rebates) rather than only punitive approaches to protect recharge areas, floodplains, and water bodies. Emerging examples of BGI integration in master plans (of Delhi and other cities) demonstrate how planning norms can be rewritten to keep hydrological functions central to urban form (Rajput 2020; DDA 2021).

Third, the protection and rejuvenation of water bodies must be institutionalized through clear mandates, mapping protocols, and financing pathways that cut across rural and urban schemes. Systematic mapping of tanks, lakes, ponds, and wetlands is a prerequisite for safeguarding them from encroachment and degradation.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 195

Lessons from the Amrit Sarovar scheme, which aimed to rejuvenate 75 water bodies in each rural district of the country, especially from projects implemented in peri-urban areas (Kanojia et al. 2024), should be studied and used to frame a policy for ULGs aimed at rejuvenating their own water bodies. Some projects were able to move beyond rejuvenation to beautification and even income generation (CMGGA Team 2024). Because RLGs often administer peri-urban areas and CTs, rural schemes can be used to map and rejuvenate local water bodies. Several projects successfully used mapping, collaboration, and capacity-building to create more resilient water systems. Here, Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) has proved to be a valuable tool for accessing funding and implementation (Appadurai et al. 2022). Frameworks such as the Urban River Management Plan (URMP) should be embedded into city- and regional-level planning processes with aligned funding streams, ensuring that river-sensitive planning is not confined to pilots.

Fourth, NbS should be mainstreamed into urban water policy rather than treated as add-ons. As a Ramsar Convention signatory, an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable utilization of wetlands, India can position urban and peri-urban wetlands as critical assets for recharge capacity and aquifer health, pollution attenuation, and flood buffering (Pandey 2024), integrating their protection into zoning, building regulations, and investment priorities. Scaling lessons from initiatives such as Shallow Aquifer Management under AMRUT 2.0

can help ULGs and parastatals institutionalize aquifer mapping, recharge structures, and community-level water access within urban spatial and environmental planning frameworks (NIUA 2024).

Fifth, stormwater and surface runoff need to be governed as resources, not nuisances. Policies and technical standards should promote separated stormwater networks, on-site detention and infiltration, and decentralized treatment and reuse (for non-potable purposes), especially in new layouts and large developments. Investing in such systems can simultaneously reduce pollutant loads in rivers, reduce groundwater stress, and improve urban flood resilience.

Finally, policy design must be informed by practical lessons from past experiments and calibrated to institutional capacity. The Bengaluru example of mandating 100 percent wastewater reuse in all large housing complexes shows that overambitious, one-size-fits-all targets can drive noncompliance and undermine credibility (Kuttuva et al. 2018). More realistic thresholds, differentiated by city size and typology, coupled with clear operations and maintenance (O&M) and monitoring arrangements, are essential. Similarly, the Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain campaign needs stronger enforcement, convergence with local planning, and monitoring of outcomes to become a meaningful vehicle for groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting, particularly in the context of rapidly falling groundwater tables and growing calls for reform as India's aquifers face severe stress.

CHAPTER 10.

# Climate Vulnerability and Resilience

The chapter examines how national policies can strengthen climate action planning at the city-region level while enabling cross-sectoral co-benefits. It addresses the urgency of multi-hazard vulnerability assessment and the challenge of integrating climate action into statutory plans. Other specific challenges unpacked include extreme urban heat, flood resilience, barriers to nature-based solutions, and a lack of adaptation thinking in urban transport. Improving urban energy efficiency to drive mitigation rounds out the discussion, with policy recommendations linking each challenge to sustainable, low-carbon urban development pathways.

An urbanization policy must place climate change at its core, urgently addressing both mitigation and adaptation as non-negotiable priorities. The 2024 Global Carbon Budget finds that carbon dioxide (CO$^{2}$) emissions from fossil use in India are set to rise by 4.6 percent (Hausfather and Friedlingstein 2024). Although the country’s historical share is low, its carbon footprint has been climbing, especially as the economy and energy-intensive industries have expanded after COVID-19 (IEA 2024).

The Climate Transparency Report, which takes stock of the climate performance of the G20, states that India is the most vulnerable of these countries to climate change (Climate Transparency 2022). In 2021, India suffered a loss of 5.4 percent of its GDP from climate events. The forecast for the near future predicts a 49 percent rise in annual damages from weather events and a 5 percent decline in labor productivity.

By 2050, India’s urban population is expected to double, with urban development driving emissions upward. In India’s larger cities, synthesis across multiple city GHG (greenhouse gas) inventories and national energy data show that stationary energy use in buildings and industry typically accounts for the largest share of urban emissions, with most of this demand met by predominantly coal-based grid electricity (NIUA 2021; de Bruyn and Bhardwaj 2023; Climate Action Tracker 2025). Rapid motorization, particularly in cities, has made the transport sector the third-largest contributor to CO$^{2}$ emissions in India (IEA 2023).

The GoI recognizes environmental protection as a key element of sustainable urbanization. India is a signatory to multiple international agreements to steer India toward a low-carbon, resource-efficient, and sustainable future, including the SDGs, the Paris Agreement, the Quito Declaration on Sustainable Cities and Human Settlements for All, the International Solar Alliance, and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Host Country Agreement, among others. India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement commit to achieving net zero emissions by 2070, a 45 percent decrease in the emissions intensity of the economy from its 2005 levels by 2030, as well as a cumulative 50 percent share of electric power installed capacity for non-fossil-fuel sources. The latter two targets were updated in 2023 because the earlier targets, a 33–35 percent reduction in emissions intensity and 40 percent installed capacity for non-fossil-fuel energy, were achieved in 2023, according to the GoI (MoEFCC 2023).

The current phase of India’s attempt to deal with climate change can be traced back to 2007 when the Prime Minister’s Council on Climate Change (PMCCC) was established.

A year later, the Council published the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), which recognizes the cross-sectoral nature of the climate problem and tries to address it through eight missions (see Figure 43). Even though the MoEFCC is the nodal ministry of climate change, different line ministries are responsible for each mission under NAPCC (see Figure 43). Several of the NAPCC missions have a bearing on urbanization, such as the National Solar Mission (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy), National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (Bureau of Energy Efficiency), National Mission for Sustainable Habitat (MoHUA), National Water Mission (Ministry of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation), and National Mission for Strategic Knowledge on Climate Change (MoEFCC).

India’s efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change in urban areas have expanded significantly over the past two decades. These initiatives include climate action plans, urban adaptation strategies, and resilience plans to help cities cope with climate impacts. Specific action plans have been developed to mitigate heat and flood risks. The NDMA, which promotes localized and context-specific strategies for managing hazards in Indian cities, often guides these efforts. They align with national and subnational climate goals and fit within the broader framework of climate policy and action, but are not actively supported by them because urban climate action has not been a primary focus of higher levels of government.

Importantly, urban climate change efforts can often fall between the cracks of larger planning efforts. The 2020 ClimateSmart Cities Assessment Framework (CSCAF), within the SCM (NIUA 2020), illustrates how this could occur. Led by MoHUA, the framework has raised awareness of climate vulnerability in urban planning, but its scope is limited. It underscores the tension in India’s urban climate efforts, because MoEFCC is not responsible for urban issues, and MoHUA often overlooks climate-related concerns in its urban plans and programs.

Limited support from the GoI has led urban climate action planning in India to increasingly rely on collaboration with international networks and seek financial assistance from diverse sources. These initiatives engage local urban governments, various NGOs, and other non-state actors, such as consultants, experts, and academics. Help is also received from national and international donors and formal city consortia (Khosla and Bharadwaj 2019). This collaboration began with organizations such as ICLEI – Local Governments for Sustainability and the Asian Cities Climate Change Resilience Network (ACCCRN), which is funded by the Rockefeller Foundation (Sharma et al. 2014).

Currently, six Indian cities are part of the C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group and are either developing or have recently published their city climate action plans to align with C40 leadership standards. Additionally, NIUA has developed four Climate Action Plans based on the CSCAF Framework for four cities: Leh, Pune, Jamnagar, and Junagadh. Although the experiences of these cities have varied, their participation has spurred new climate-focused initiatives, including vulnerability assessments and the ongoing creation of climate action plans for the involved cities.

Under its NDCs, India has pledged to create an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO$_{2}$ by increasing forest and tree cover by 2030. The National Biodiversity Action Plan includes a chapter on urban biodiversity and calls for protecting biodiversity and ecosystems in urban settings through land-use planning and regulations (MoEFCC 2019). NbS can buffer urbanizing areas against the impacts of climate change and support these policies in achieving their goals. These projects harness the potential of nature and natural processes to protect and restore ecosystems and enhance the services they offer. They also tackle societal challenges such as food and water security, disaster risk reduction, and biodiversity conservation. National programs, such as PMAY and AMRUT, can support urban NbS and initiatives such as urban forest creation and lake restoration, fostering climate resilient urban development.

Although there is an extensive set of national policies, guidelines, and laws with the potential to contribute to city-level NbS projects, specific frameworks and policies for implementing urban NbS do not exist in India. COP30 catalyzed the Beat the Heat initiative, with 185 cities committing to tackle urban extreme heat using measures such as trees, parks, urban forests, and wetlands (van den Berg 2025).

## Challenges and Recommendations

### Challenge 1

**Multi-hazard climate vulnerability burdens Indian cities and city regions, but their statutory plans lack climate resilient planning frameworks. In addition, city climate action plans lack statutory backing and are currently restricted to municipal boundaries.**

A host of factors contribute to India’s climate vulnerability, including the lack of timely, reliable, and localized data on climate, weather, multi-hazard risks, and vulnerability (Mohanty 2020), which hampers proactive and context-specific resilient planning.

There is an urgent need for data and tools that can identify the most probable and severe scenarios of future urbanization and climate variability over the short, medium, and long term (Rangwala et al. 2024).

Current vulnerability assessments for risk-informed planning often focus too narrowly on physical exposure to hazards, discounting the socioeconomic and institutional factors that shape how different people and communities experience climate impacts (Rangwala et al. 2024). Effective resilience demands tools that capture probable climate and urbanization scenarios across time scales, incorporating both physical hazards and socioeconomic, institutional vulnerabilities to reflect unequal risks among populations. Current assessments often overlook these complexities, resulting in piecemeal strategies. Although the NAPCC promotes research and capacity-building, urban vulnerability assessments seldom inform statutory planning frameworks robustly.

Recent city-scale initiatives, such as WRI India’s Climate Resilient Cities work and the Climate Hazard and Vulnerability Assessment (CHVA) framework for Indian cities, demonstrate how comprehensive vulnerability assessments can integrate spatial climate hazard data (including information on heat, flooding, landslides, and other risks) with socioeconomic indicators, housing and infrastructure conditions, and access to services. This approach allows for mapping differential vulnerability across neighborhoods and prioritizing interventions for the most at-risk communities. However, experiences from cities such as Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kochi, and Nashik reveal that such frameworks demand extensive geospatial, demographic, and sectoral datasets, along with iterative analysis. This highlights how far many Indian cities still are from achieving the data and institutional capacities necessary for routine, equity-centered vulnerability assessments and climate-informed planning.

Institutionally, poor vertical coordination between central, state, and local governments, coupled with weak horizontal integration across urban agencies, undermines cohesive climate governance (King and Naidoo 2025). Climate risks transcend administrative boundaries, necessitating aligned policies and joint action across city regions. Although multiple NAPCC missions and national urban schemes (e.g., National Mission on Sustainable Habitat, AMRUT, and the SCM) target green infrastructure, mobility, water, and waste, their efforts remain siloed. Specialized agencies seldom synchronize objectives into unified statutory master plans and regional plans, diluting impact and efficiency.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 201

# Recommendation 1

### **Embed multi-hazard, data-driven, equity-focused resilience planning in statutory plans. Strengthen data systems.**

A national- and state-level database of climate- and air-pollution-related risks and hazards should be developed to guide future urban growth and infrastructure decisions. This database must capture elements at risk—specific population groups, critical infrastructure, and economic sectors—and cover meteorological, hydrological, geological, and environmental hazards, with information disaggregated by geography, ecological zone, season, and vulnerable locations and populations. Knowledge networks created under the National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change should be leveraged to build this multi-hazard, equity-aware evidence base for urban areas.

Good practices such as utilizing Yale's Urban Environment and Social Inclusion Index (UESI) can inform the development of a climate and environmental risk index that provides urban residents, city managers, and policymakers with fine-grained data on city performance on key climate and inclusion metrics. The UESI demonstrates how high-resolution, large-scale datasets can be used to assess whether cities are meeting goals for sustainable and inclusive growth, and similar approaches could underpin a national climate risk and resilience index for Indian cities (Data-Driven EnviroLab 2024).

Verifiable, interoperable, and publicly accessible data should be integrated into the National Urban Information System (NUIS) and updated regularly. Public access will be crucial for enabling communities, civil society, and local governments to use this information to plan, prepare, and allocate resources for resilience. Existing data infrastructure created through national initiatives—such as Integrated Command and Control Centres under the SCM, the India Urban Data Exchange, and the National Data and Analytics Platform—should be systematically aligned with resilience objectives, actively promoted, and supported by feedback loops that capture how cities are using data for climate action.

All statutory plans for urban development should mandate the use of vulnerability assessments that consider multiple hazards and the socioeconomic, institutional, and spatial dimensions of vulnerability. Well-maintained national and state data repositories, developed in partnership with state agencies, should provide standardized exposure and vulnerability indicators for all districts and metropolitan regions. This would enable robust city-level baseline assessments and periodic updates as climate risks evolve and cities grow. Recent tools, including WRI India's CHVA framework and related climate action planning in cities such as Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kochi, Nashik, Solapur, and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, show both the potential and the data intensity of rigorous, equity-centered vulnerability assessments and underscore the need to strengthen local capacities and institutional mandates for such work (see Figure 44).

## Challenge 2

### Extreme heat events and rising heat stress put millions of urban residents at risk in India, yet heat has not been recognized as a national disaster.

Prolonged and extreme heat conditions continue to become more common worldwide. The World Meteorological Organization, based on six international datasets, has confirmed that 2024 is the warmest year on record, at about 1.55°C above the pre-industrial level (World Meteorological Organization 2025). WRI analyzed annual days where maximum temperatures exceed 35°C (95°F), and found that at 1.5°C of warming, only 67 cities will experience 150 or more days a year of temperatures exceeding 35°C; under 3°C of warming, this rises to 197 cities. More than half of those cities (103) are in India (Mackres et al. 2023).

WRI India’s research reveals that millions of Indians are not only exposed to dangerously high temperatures but also face prolonged exposure (Palanichamy 2022).

A number of factors contribute to increasing heat stress in cities: high densities, low vegetation, and the choice of construction materials have all been shown to exacerbate the UHI effect, which leads to significant heat stress in urban areas (Deilami et al. 2018; Agarwal et al. 2022; Mackres et al. 2024).

By 2017, heat-exposed labor accounted for 50 percent of India’s GDP and employed about 75 percent of the workforce (McKinsey Global Institute 2010). Informal settlements, where many urban residents live, experience even higher heat stress—up to six degrees hotter than average—making residents especially vulnerable (Chatterjee 2020). This increased heat also disproportionately harms informal workers such as street vendors, affecting their health and livelihoods (Ghosh 2024).

Some of the current methods used by government agencies to measure climate vulnerability do not account for heat stress. For instance, the GoI currently uses a Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) to measure climate vulnerability, but it does not include indicators of heat stress. A 2023 study (Debnath et al. 2023) showed that although 45 percent of India is rated moderately vulnerable by CVI, applying a Heat Index (HI) would place over 90 percent

of the country in the “Extreme Caution” or “Danger” categories. Even states with a “Low” CVI rank are placed in the “Danger” category by the HI, indicating that heat vulnerability is underestimated.

The policy response and actions in India center around “heat waves,” because such events over the past decade have led to significant loss of life. However, the National Disaster Management Act (DMA) 2005 does not designate heat waves as disasters. Instead, the major policy response to heat waves has come in the form of subnational Heat Action Plans (HAPs) at the state, district, and ULG levels to reduce heat-related mortality. Beginning with Ahmedabad in 2013, several cities, districts, and states have prepared HAPs in recent years. A comprehensive analysis of 37 HAPs across the country (Pillai and Dalal 2023) found several key takeaways on the state of heat policy in India. One of the major challenges is an oversimplified view of heat waves that fails to account for local context.

For instance, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) declares a heat wave if the maximum temperature exceeds a certain threshold, which can vary according to terrain, for two consecutive days. However, localized factors such as humidity or windspeed also affect the perceived temperature, causing discomfort and health impacts that might not be captured by temperature alone. Analysis by CPR showed that as of March 2023, only 10 out of 37 HAPs considered locally defined temperature thresholds (Sangomla 2023). HAPs also fail to adequately target the most vulnerable groups.

Current approaches to heat vulnerability in India emphasize heat waves and their direct mortality risks, overlooking the broader health and productivity impacts that occur at temperatures just below official thresholds, as well as the exacerbating effects of rising nighttime heat and humidity. Figure 45 shows how heat absorbed by built landscapes during the day is released at night, resulting in sustained heat exposure, in cities like Delhi. This narrow framing treats heat vulnerability as a temporary issue tied to discrete “heat wave” events with defined start and end points, rather than an ongoing condition during prolonged periods of extreme heat (Khandekar et al. 2024). Moreover, heat-related policies remain poorly integrated with other sectors, and insufficient systematic attention is paid to addressing heat risks across multiple spatial scales—from neighborhoods to cities—and governance levels.

## Recommendation 2

**Heat (not just heat waves) must be considered a national disaster, supported by policies and legal frameworks at the national level to enable effective action at the local and regional levels.**

Extreme heat events are fundamentally reshaping the living and working conditions of people, as well as natural ecosystems and resources. India must act both urgently and incrementally to address heat risks across regions and sectors and transition to a path where people and ecosystems can adapt and thrive, and loss of lives and productivity during extreme heat is mitigated. The formation of a high-level committee to consult and advise on the many dimensions of heat risks and impacts across sectors on workers, productivity, housing, infrastructures, and ecosystems could be a first step toward addressing the major shifts extreme heat is poised to trigger.

Several states, including Tamil Nadu (*The Hindu* 2024), Madhya Pradesh (*The Economic Times* 2024), and Telangana (Pisharody 2025), have declared heat waves a disaster, requiring state disaster response funds to be used for relief expenditure. However, funds from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) are inaccessible because heat is not a designated a disaster nationally. A key focus should be to establish stronger legal and institutional foundations for heat-related initiatives, which will allow governments at all levels to act with greater intention and effectiveness. Classifying heat as a natural disaster at the national level will allow states to use national disaster relief funds to address extreme events and provide relief.

Creating regionally relevant heat thresholds can help local governments improve preparation and action during extreme heat periods. Heat action and relief can be disbursed in accordance with the needs of the region rather than limited to the universal thresholds that are currently used to declare heat waves a disaster. Physiological response to heat is influenced by an interplay of meteorological factors and individual adaptive capacities. For vulnerable communities, these capacities are severely constrained by occupational exposure, housing quality, access to cooling, physiological vulnerability, water and sanitation insecurity, economic limitations, and information asymmetry. Traditional heat thresholds or generalized HI values may not adequately reflect the perceived and physiological heat stress experienced by these groups, particularly when compounded by high humidity, lack of recovery at night, and physical exertion. Therefore, a context-specific assessment is imperative. The larger outcome from the regional heat thresholds framework and operationalization would help inform policy, enhance adaptive capacities, improve public health, and build economic resilience to heat. Meanwhile, integrating HAPs into statutory plans and policies such as city-level master plans, development

plans, and climate action plans will make it easier for city governments to identify and draw on the required funding. For example, WRI India conducted a “budget-tagging” exercise in which specific budget items in the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation budget were identified for implementing the action tracks of the Mumbai Climate Action Plan. This exercise leveraged about 75 percent of the Garden Department’s budget for scientific greening as a critical heat adaptation measure of the city (see Box 22).

Development under current urbanization models contributes to the UHI effect by prioritizing built-up areas at the expense of vegetation and permeability. Cities and states should establish guidelines for preserving green cover in transitional areas because they play a crucial role in balancing urban expansion with environmental sustainability. These spaces are crucial for temperature regulation and UHI mitigation: WRI research has shown that there is a strong relationship between green cover and land surface temperature, with a difference of 5.5°C between different parts of Mumbai (Mackres et al. 2024).

Building characteristics also contribute to indoor heat conditions, which are an understudied, invisible risk, disproportionately affecting home-based workers, children, and the elderly. Critical attention must be focused on improving housing and building profiles to deliver thermally comfortable living and working conditions by working with housing boards and slum rehabilitation agencies. Demonstrated effective solutions include cool roofs to reduce heat absorption, incorporating design that optimizes natural ventilation through design (Mahila Housing SEWA Trust et al. 2025) and provides for open and green spaces in informal housing layouts (Mahadevia et al. 2020). These local, low-cost, and passive design interventions should be prioritized over energy-consuming technologies. Such cooling technologies, when used, should be complemented by efforts at improving energy efficiency and diversifying the energy mix. This is discussed in detail in the section of this chapter titled “Challenge 6.”

In addition, engaging development authorities at the level of the metropolitan region, such as the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority and BMRDA, to bring together heat-related action across the metropolitan region is important.

Finally, integration at the national level will also bring disparate efforts together, enabling collaboration and synergy. Several researchers, CSOs, and private-sector organizations are involved in developing new methods, materials, and strategies to study and address extreme heat in indoor and outdoor conditions. A national-level forum convened by the GoI with diverse stakeholders will allow this work to move forward together.
