## Recommendation 2

### Hard-wire OSR and predictable transfers into the municipal finance architecture.

An NUP should align revenue expenditure with constitutionally assigned functions by incentivizing systematic OSR growth and ensuring predictable, formula-based intergovernmental transfers. Building on the trajectory from the 13th to the 16th FCs, this alignment must explicitly aim to reduce structural dependence on ad hoc grants; treat property tax, land based instruments, and user charges as the primary pillars of municipal finance; and embed climate resilience and environmental sustainability into the design of both OSR instruments and transfers.

The GoI must incentivize states to synchronize activity mapping for their ULGs with functional assignments, so that every function entrusted to ULGs is backed by commensurate and regular fiscal devolution. This must be done at the same time that the lines of accountability between ULGs and parastatals are being clarified (as mentioned in Recommendation 1 above) and includes establishing service-level agreements and ensuring transparent financial flows for water supply, sewerage, public transport, and SWM.

This functional clarity must be complemented by greater authority to raise and manage revenues. The GoI should encourage municipal finance frameworks that operationalize the principles of “Users Pay,” “Beneficiaries Pay,” and “Polluter Pays.” Beyond taxation, ULGs should systematically deploy land-based financing—including land monetization and LVC—as significant sources of OSR. ULGs should levy development and improvement charges to build and maintain infrastructure in return for allowing higher intensity of economic activity and land use within their boundaries (Rithmire 2015).

To strengthen OSR to service better-quality urbanization, states must turn planning decisions into predictable revenue through LVC, strengthen the property tax base, link land development to infrastructure financing, create earmarked politically visible funds, and adapt financial tools for small and transitional settlements (see Box 25 for details).

Predictability in financial transfers is equally crucial. The central and state FCs could design and implement a formula for fiscal transfers based on objective indicators such as the per capita cost of service provision, population and population density, urbanization dynamics, fiscal effort and OSR performance, and environmental and climate vulnerability. This will ensure that urbanizing areas receive a predictable and equitable share of resources. Furthermore, FCs and state governments should implement adequate measures to eliminate or reduce the prevalent bias toward metros and large cities.

To this end, FCs and state governments should institutionalize annual needs assessments and fiscal gap analyses for ULGs, and use them to calibrate both vertical and horizontal devolution. This will create a more balanced and predictable municipal finance framework, under which ULGs with weaker tax bases—but that make credible efforts to improve OSR and financial management—receive proportionately higher support, while better off and better performing ULGs are nudged toward greater self reliance and market finance.

Comprehensive municipal finance reforms are especially urgent for non-metropolitan cities, where fragmented mandates, weak tax handles, and irregular transfers constrain both service delivery and climate resilience. An NUP should hard-wire predictable intergovernmental transfers, systematic OSR enhancement (especially property tax, LVC, and user charges), and capital market access into the municipal finance architecture, with tailored support for non-metropolitan cities, where OSR finances barely 37–42 percent of revenue expenditure. Such a policy must explicitly differentiate between million plus municipal corporations and smaller ULGs, given the latter’s much higher dependence (57–61 percent) on state and central transfers (Gupta et al. 2025).

The Union Budget 2026–27 signals a welcome shift toward market-based urban financing by proposing an INR 1 billion incentive for single municipal bond issuances above INR 10 billion, while continuing the AMRUT-linked support for smaller issuances (Ministry of Finance 2026). This measure reduces effective borrowing costs for creditworthy Municipal Corporations and nudges them to move beyond a narrow dependence on taxes, fees, and intergovernmental transfers toward more diversified financing. Properly designed, large, project-linked bonds can push ULGs to strengthen their balance sheets, improve credit ratings, ring-fence cash flows, and rationalize user charges, thereby deepening stable OSR streams and weaning ULGs from episodic fee increases (Athar et al. 2022). However, municipal bonds are debt, not income; without parallel reforms in property tax, user charges, accounting, and governance, they could simply add repayment pressures. Moreover, only a small group of large cities currently meet the thresholds of financial health and institutional capacity needed for such issuances, limiting their near-term, system-wide impact (CareEdge Ratings 2025). The recent return of unutilized bond proceeds by Pune Municipal Corporation after nearly seven years highlights that creditworthiness alone does not guarantee successful deployment; robust project pipelines, procurement capacity, and timely contract management are equally critical.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 239

A serious agenda for augmenting OSR must therefore pair bond incentives with structural reforms in local taxation, cost-reflective tariffs, and predictable intergovernmental

transfers, so that capital market access becomes both a reward for, and a driver of, durable fiscal strengthening at the ULG level (Accountability Initiative 2023).

# BOX 25 | Strengthening own source revenue (OSR) for delivering better-quality urbanization

- **Turn planning decisions into predictable revenue.** When regional and local plans clearly designate growth corridors, higher intensity zones, and serviced layouts, urban local governments (ULGs) can levy betterment charges, impact fees, or premium FAR charges on developments that benefit from public investments, converting plan-driven land value gains into recurring or one-time municipal revenues rather than windfalls for private owners.
- **Strengthen the property tax base.** Robust property tax databases that integrate a detailed, spatially referenced property database with tax and building permission systems, as in Surat, allow ULGs to systematically update assessments when land use intensifies or new layouts are approved, ensuring that rising land and building values are reflected in property tax collections. In transitional areas, coupling land value capture (LVC) instruments (e.g., charges on subdivision or regularization) with immediate inclusion in the property register can bring large parts of peri-urban growth into the tax net.
- **Linking land development to infrastructure financing.** Where town planning schemes, guided land development, or pooling/readjustment models are used, the ULG can reserve and subsequently auction or lease a portion of the reconstituted plots, but with clear safeguards to prevent displacement and to cross-subsidize upgrading in informal and low income areas. The proceeds should be earmarked not only for local roads, drainage, parks, and climate resilient infrastructure in new growth areas, but also for in situ upgrading, basic services, and risk reduction investments in existing informal settlements that have historically received little public investment. This links land value gains to redistribution, so that better infrastructure raises values and expands future LVC and property tax potential while simultaneously improving living conditions for the most vulnerable residents.
- **Create earmarked politically visible funds.** Political support for earmarking LVC grows when residents and representatives can clearly see direct, local returns from these revenues. If LVC is systematically channeled into highly visible neighborhood improvements—better roads, drains that reduce flooding, street lighting, parks, and climate resilient upgrades—communities can connect new changes to tangible benefits, including in informal and low-income areas. Publishing simple ward-level statements of “LVC collected versus investments delivered” and pairing them with matching funds from higher tiers allows councilors and Members of Legislative Assembly to claim credit for expanding local resources through formal, rule-based land transactions rather than opaque deals.
- **Adapt tools for small and transitional settlements.** In transitional areas with weak land records and limited administrative capacity, ULGs can start with very simple rule based instruments that are easy to administer. Examples include standardized layout approval fees explicitly tied to providing basic access roads and drains, or modest betterment charges on formally regularized plots. Even these basic tools can incrementally expand OSR while building routines for recording and updating properties. As cadastral information and property databases become more complete and reliable, these interim instruments can gradually be upgraded into more sophisticated LVC and property tax systems.

Source: WRI India authors.

## Challenge 3

### Inadequate institutional arrangements for regional planning and governance to address the rural–urban continuum resulting from urbanization.

As Indian cities expand and grow, they can potentially benefit from agglomeration networks. However, Indian cities largely experience outward horizontal growth with low-rise development, much like pancakes. Fragmented property rights, restrictive zoning, and dysfunctional land markets, along with policy constraints that limit vertical expansion by suppressing infill and height, encourage sprawl into peri-urban areas (Lall et al. 2021). Pancake-style urban development encourages low-rise sprawl in peri-urban areas (see Figure 54) and creates governance voids through jurisdictional mismatches between Municipal Corporations, state development authorities, and rural Panchayats, causing overlapping mandates, weak coordination, and limited local accountability. This leads to inadequate planning and infrastructure development across the region and failure to cater to the needs of transitional urban areas and undertake preparatory planning for future urbanization.

The 74th CAA envisions MPCs, but their implementation has been poor. In many cases, they are advisory bodies without any real teeth. Parastatal agencies continue to undertake most of the regional planning work (see Box 26). However, these bodies operate with limited accountability to local populations, and their responsibilities often

overlap with municipal functions. In practice, large projects (highways, industrial parks, land development) are decided by higher-level authorities (state or central) with little horizontal coordination.

Moreover, existing laws fail to adequately recognize the rural–urban continuum that characterizes urbanization in India, leaving peri-urban and transitional spaces under planned and poorly governed. Constitutional and legal frameworks still treat “rural” and “urban” as mutually exclusive, with Panchayats and municipalities operating in parallel rather than through integrated metropolitan or regional structures, even though labor, land, infrastructure, and environmental systems now cut across these boundaries. This binary is reinforced by the distinction between CTs and STs and by state laws that focus on individual ULG limits rather than functional regions, producing fragmented authority over transport, land use, water, and environmental regulation at the urban fringe. Transitional areas—CTs, OGs, and prospective Nagar Panchayats—often fall between planning regimes: they lack statutory town planning instruments, metropolitan-scale bodies, or clear mandates for coordinating Gram Panchayats and municipalities on issues such as sprawl, floodplains, aquifers, and regional infrastructure corridors. Existing experiments, such as Odisha’s rural–urban transition architecture and Rajasthan’s proposed multitier transition councils and settlement cells, are important but state specific; there

is still no legally enforceable framework for regional transition governance that can systematically handle cross-jurisdictional dynamics. As a result, decisions to upgrade or de-notify areas remain highly political and piecemeal, driven more by administrative convenience and local power dynamics than by coherent regional plans. Courts largely confine themselves to checking procedural legality rather than the suitability of regional governance arrangements (Malhotra and Kapur 2025).

Additionally, state-level town and country planning legislation generally does not provide for effective regional planning. For instance, the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act (1973) lacks provisions for regional planning, and the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act (1967) limits regional planning boards to advisory roles. Only a few states, such as Tamil Nadu, under the Town and Country Planning Act (1971), have comparatively stronger provisions for regional planning. This fragmented legal framework results in ambiguous governance arrangements. Within city boundaries, ULGs are constitutionally recognized as local governments, but their powers are often constrained by state laws, financial dependence, and overlapping mandates with state departments and parastatal agencies, which together allow state governments to retain significant control over city governance. In areas outside city limits, rural governance institutions formally hold jurisdiction, but their authority is often superseded by state-level parastatals once these areas are designated for development. This does not necessarily strip local representatives of their decision-making voice, but it does require them to operate within new forums that are structurally aligned with state government control.

In addition, this structure of regional planning and coordination is suboptimal from the point of view of planning itself. The Indian Constitution assigns master planning to ULGs and delegates regional planning responsibilities to MPCs and DPCs. However, these bodies often lack the necessary spatial planning expertise. Planning capacity sits elsewhere, in parastatals and state government departments (see Box 26 for the example of Mumbai). This is the case in states such as Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, and Sikkim (Parmar et al. 2024).

The current structure of regional planning and coordination is not working. The URDPFI guidelines categorize planning regions into three types: administrative regions, investment regions, and special regions. Regional development authorities manage metropolitan regional planning and assist smaller ULGs that lack planning capacity. In contrast, SPVs oversee investment regions and operate independently of local authorities. Currently, only a few planning authorities have creatively leveraged existing planning and governance structures to promote balanced territorial development.

### BOX 26 | How the MMPC and MMRDA function in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region

The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA, 1974) retains primary control over regional infrastructure investments (e.g., metro rail, skywalks, rental housing). The Mumbai Metropolitan Planning Committee (MMPC), constituted in 2009 to meet the 74th Constitutional Amendment's mandate for metropolitan-level coordination, has limited de facto authority: it does not command capital budgets, rarely arbitrates inter-jurisdictional trade-offs, and exerts little influence over project sequencing.

As a result, planning remains predominantly top-down and fragmented across municipalities; genuine cross-municipal coordination is the exception and typically occurs through the MMRDA's initiatives rather than being directed by the MMPC. This illustrates a persistent design-implementation gap: institutions for coordination exist on paper, but their powers, resourcing, and use are insufficient to deliver integrated regional planning.

Source: Pethe et al. 2011.

## Recommendation 3

Create institutional frameworks for regional planning. Explore pathways to provide municipal services to CTs and urbanizing villages in the peripheries of large cities as part of an integrated urban system.

State governments should revise the Town and Country Planning Acts to explicitly recognize and provide for continuous urban regions, including peri-urban areas and CTs. Revising these laws will enable a more integrated approach to urban expansion, ensuring that planning mechanisms reflect the realities of spatial and economic growth.

CTs, which exhibit urban characteristics and are classified as “urban” for data enumeration purposes, continue to be administered by rural governments. In India, the functions of ULGs and RLGs are defined, by the 11th Schedule of the 73rd CAA and the 12th Schedule of the 74th CAA. Although both ULGs and RLGs focus on local governance and service delivery, ULGs have far more complex roles, given their higher population density, greater infrastructural complexity, pressing environmental concerns, and the economic diversity of urban areas. Additional responsibilities of ULGs include comprehensive

244

WRI-INDIA.ORG

urban infrastructure management (such as piped water, sewerage networks, multi-modal transportation, and SWM), planning and building regulations, advanced public health facilities, environmental management, civic amenities (such as parks, libraries, and recreation areas), poverty alleviation programs, and regulatory activities (such as licensing of businesses, markets, street vending, and traffic management). See Table 23 for a summary of the responsibilities of ULGs and RLGs.

As rural areas transition from farm to nonfarm activities and densify without proper services and infrastructure, India needs policies and institutional arrangements to support emerging urbanization, where economic urbanization is outpacing physical urbanization. There is an urgent need to analyze the reality of peri-urban, rural, and urban areas, and CTs to understand the nature of changes and aspirations and recommend pathways through which synchronization can be built around rural and urban governance functions to service these emerging urban spaces.

The framework of recommendations presented in this report recognizes that implementation pathways will differ across India's system of cities; however, capacity deficits in smaller ULGs and CTs need to be foregrounded as a central equity concern rather than a background constraint. Explicitly linking their deficits to the proposed governance reforms can clarify how institutional changes translate into real gains on the ground. Proposals such as state level municipal service commissions, permanent middle-level and frontline staffing, and dedicated urban cadres are not simply bureaucratic refinements; they are preconditions for smaller towns to prepare and enforce spatial plans, manage assets, and engage meaningfully with regional and district scale planning processes. Similarly, when finance–function alignment and predictable transfers first target the most capacity constrained ULGs and transitional bodies, the NUP may narrow rather than widen disparities in service quality between large cities and smaller urban settlements.

For areas outside metropolitan or designated planning boundaries, this capacity lens needs to extend to district level and regional institutions as well. A district planning approach that includes peri-urban areas, new towns, greenfield townships, transitional settlements, and rural outskirts helps support metropolitan economies. This approach allows for the recognition and planning of important roles, such as labor markets, transport hubs, and service centers, even in areas with limited resources. Kollam's Integrated District Development Plan shows how spatial, participatory, and multi-level planning can be organized so that weaker local bodies are supported by stronger district and metropolitan institutions while balancing top-down vision with bottom-up action—an essential lesson for other Indian states aiming to strengthen decentralized district planning and integrated regional governance (see Box 27).

#### BOX 27 | Kollam's Integrated District Development Plan

Kollam's Integrated District Development Plan (IDDP) represents a pioneering initiative in Kerala that blends spatial analysis, participatory governance, and a long-term vision to guide district-wide development. As the only district in the state with a sanctioned IDDP rooted in spatial planning, Kollam offers valuable lessons for regional planning across India.

At the heart of Kollam's IDDP is a spatially grounded approach that integrates urban and rural development. The plan encompasses land-use zoning, circulation networks, and civic infrastructure, supported by detailed mapping and evidence-based assessments of local resources and needs. This spatial lens ensures that development is not only systematic but also responsive to the district's geographic and socioeconomic realities. Functioning as an overarching blueprint, the IDDP aligns the priorities of all Local Self Government Institutions (LSGIs), including Panchayats and Municipalities. Each LSGI formulates its own development plan in harmony with the district's vision, fostering coherence, reducing duplication, and enhancing the efficiency of public investments.

The IDDP articulates a 20-year development vision, operationalized through phased action plans—typically in five-year increments. Community engagement is embedded throughout the planning process. Working groups comprising elected representatives, sectoral experts, and citizens contribute to data collection, concept development, and proposal formulation. This participatory ethos ensures that the plan reflects lived realities and local aspirations, enhancing its legitimacy and relevance. The IDDP addresses a wide spectrum of development domains: economic growth, basic services (water, sanitation, energy), infrastructure, environmental stewardship, and natural resource management. This thematic comprehensiveness supports a holistic and sustainable development trajectory. Execution mechanisms include detailed zoning regulations, phased improvements to road and transport networks, and targeted interventions for slum upgrading and economic development. These tools provide both structure and flexibility, enabling responsive and orderly implementation.

Source: Government of Kerala 2008.

Source: WRI India authors.

A comprehensive urbanization policy directs integrated development across urban, peri-urban, and rural areas to prepare for economic development and spatial transformation. The Kerala Urban Policy Commission (2025-2050) has recommended setting up six directly elected MPCs around the Municipal Corporations of Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode, Kollam, Thrissur, and Kannur to steer the process of urban development in and around these areas. It further requests that the state government support the MPCs and DPCs by establishing planning departments at each metropolitan and district level, mandating the preparation of both Metropolitan Development Plans and District Development Plans as spatial development plans.

Greater Hyderabad is in the middle of a major restructuring in which peri-urban areas between the current Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) limits and the Outer Ring Road (ORR) are being brought under unified metropolitan planning and municipal governance. The Telangana government has approved the merger of 27 peripheral ULGs located within the ORR into the GHMC, expanding the corporation's jurisdiction from about 650 km² to around 2,000 km² so that the entire area up to the ORR is governed as one metropolitan corporation (Bommala 2025). Alongside municipalities, 51 Gram Panchayats in Rangareddy, Medchal Malkajgiri, and Sangareddy districts are being

merged with nearby municipalities and then effectively brought into the GHMC urban agglomeration, targeting fast-urbanizing villages that were previously outside formal urban governance (Bommala 2024). At the metropolitan scale, Hyderabad uses a relatively consolidated metropolitan planning authority (HMDA). The unified Metropolitan Development Plan 2031 includes land use zoning (including a designated peri-urban use zone) to manage transition areas and control density, coverage, and layout approvals along growth corridors. It intends to bring future peri-urban growth corridors within a statutory regional planning framework covering all subsequent extensions of the Hyderabad Metropolitan Region up to the Regional Ring Road (RRR), along with a 2-km buffer outside the RRR that can be designated and managed as an integrated growth corridor. It covers about 10,472 km² and 1,355 revenue villages across 11 districts, rather than allowing purely revenue-village-driven sprawl (HMDA 2025). The RRR and plans for radial links and metro and regional transit connections are being framed as multi-modal infrastructure backbones for these peripheral areas, aiming to integrate suburban and peri-urban settlements functionally with the city's core employment and service nodes (Balasubramanian 2024). The HMDA plan introduces a Peri Urban Zone all along the urban edge and growth corridors, with lower permissible coverage and a mix of agricultural, open, and low-intensity urban uses, explicitly recognizing the rural-to-urban transition belt.

246 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

Hyderabad’s radial–concentric structure, ORR, and growth corridors are embedded in the land use plan, with HMDA leading comprehensive transport studies and a forthcoming Comprehensive Mobility Plan 2050 tied to the development plan (*Deccan Chronicle* 2025).

Uniform national standards—for settlement classification, minimum planning instruments, and core financial reporting—provide a common floor, while support packages, staffing norms, and technical assistance must be differentiated by town size class, functional role, and position within metropolitan or district planning systems. Recommendations such as Kerala’s proposal to establish directly elected MPCs, backed by dedicated planning departments at the metropolitan and district levels and

mandatory Metropolitan and District Development Plans, illustrate how higher-tier institutions can be designed to both steer and support local governments with limited capacity. At the same time, Hyderabad’s ongoing consolidation of multiple peripheral ULGs and Gram Panchayats into a single metropolitan corporation, anchored in a unified Metropolitan Development Plan with a designated peri-urban zone and regional transport backbone, demonstrates how bringing fast-urbanizing villages and corridors into a statutory metropolitan planning and governance framework can turn fragmented capacity into a more coherent platform for implementing NUP objectives.

# Challenge 4

## Severe capacity shortfalls afflict urban governance institutions.

Many ULGs struggle with insufficient human resources, inadequate technical skills, and weak institutional systems. This capacity deficit undermines the ability of cities to plan effectively, implement infrastructure projects on time, and manage complex service delivery systems (Ghosh et al. 2014). The lack of empowerment at the local government level, fiscal resource constraints, and the dispersed accountability systems in Indian urban governance all contribute to this problem.

The CAG's 2024 report audited 18 states and found that in 16 of them, ULGs have "limited or no powers of recruitment." It also found that no state has devolved complete powers related to initiating disciplinary action and promotions (CAG 2024b). The report also finds the most acute capacity shortfalls in municipal councils, town panchayats, and poorer states. Devolution, improving financial resources, and streamlining accountability requirements will largely help address these shortfalls. A specific recommendation to map capacity requirements and build a framework for ongoing assessments is discussed below.

# Recommendation 4

## Develop a national-level framework to help and incentivize state governments to build capacity within ULGs and develop partnerships by leveraging the lessons from successful models.

A framework for capacity-building will encompass urban administration, regulation, planning, financing, and service delivery functions, addressing issues related to staffing, training, and skill development. The framework should be designed in accordance with the modern-day responsibilities of ULGs, such as working with the private sector and using GIS for master planning. States could then use this framework to determine actual staffing requirements and other resources based on the ULG-level assessment.

For resource-deficient small towns, the Odisha model has many lessons to offer. The community in Odisha's development model—especially within the Jaga Mission—served as a cornerstone for inclusive, sustainable change by serving as both beneficiaries and co-producers of urban improvement. Slum Dwellers' Associations (SDAs), Mission Shakti Groups, transgender collectives, and ragpickers' groups became active "partners" alongside ULGs, forming what is called a "fourth tier" of urban governance. These groups helped identify needs, planned infrastructure upgrades, maintained public assets, monitored progress, and ensured accountability in

service delivery, securing ownership and socioeconomic empowerment at the neighborhood level. Institutionalizing community involvement (SDAs, Mission Shakti Groups, Swachha Sathis, Jal Sathis) led to real empowerment: land rights, decision-making authority, capacity-building, and sustainable livelihoods (Vathanan and Dasgupta 2025).

The Odisha Urban Academy (OUA), which was established in 2021 under the Housing & Urban Development Department to address gaps in human capital and provide comprehensive training on urban administration, service delivery, and governance, especially benefits smaller urban centers (Government of Odisha 2021). OUA operates both as a physical institution and a digital platform (developed with Qwge Technologies), offering interactive, self-paced, and needs-based courses accessible to officials in even the remotest small towns. Training focuses on vital urban challenges such as water supply, sanitation, waste management, urban planning, municipal finance, digital service delivery, and leadership skills. Courses are regularly updated in collaboration with national and international knowledge partners such as NIUA, USAID, Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI), and Urban Management Centre (UMC), ensuring the adoption of cutting-edge practices relevant to evolving urban management needs in smaller ULGs. OUA's approach enables the inclusion of officials at all levels, from junior staff to senior administrators, across over 100 ULGs statewide, including those in smaller urban areas.

The Odisha model effectively utilized fellows from The Urban Learning Internship Programme (TULIP), a joint initiative by MoHUA and the All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE). This program places recent graduates in ULGs and Smart Cities, giving them hands-on experience in urban development while bringing fresh ideas to tackle urban challenges. In Odisha, around 2,000 TULIP fellows supported activities such as land-use mapping, compliance checks, and community engagement across 115 small cities. Their role contributed to project implementation and skill building among local officials and community leaders. The Jaga Mission showcased their impact by training community members, ensuring quality compliance, and bridging communication between authorities and residents. Odisha established the Tulip Management Unit within the Housing & Urban Development Department to manage the deployment of TULIP fellows, enhancing the impact of urban initiatives such as MUKTA, SWM, water body rejuvenation, and city digitalization projects. This coordinated approach makes Odisha a leader in leveraging youth talent in urban governance.

248 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

The Kerala Urban Policy Commission (2025–2050) has also recommended several capacity-building programs, including establishing partnerships with national and international organizations for training and retraining existing planning professionals, developing the Kerala Urban Knowledge Partnership by leveraging MoHUA’s Centre of Excellence (CoE) at NIT Calicut, and recognizing Kerala Institute of Local Administration’s (KILA) School of Urban Governance as a Centre of Excellence in urban policy and planning, tasked with capacity development for officials and elected urban representatives. It also recommended strengthening KILA’s capacity in the use of advanced geospatial technologies, data analytics tools, and funding for research to enhance decision-making and incorporate climate resilience into urban planning. Not unlike Odisha, the KUPC aims to train urban youth through the Jnanashree program to support local institutions in technology, planning, management, finance, and law.

Aggregating smaller urban places can build collaborative governance frameworks, strengthen data and technical capacity, and unlock access to larger, pooled financial resources for strategic regional development. These approaches have proved effective in diverse global contexts. The power of aggregating smaller places can be leveraged to enhance municipal capacity, improve need assessment and evidence-driven project preparation, and attract pooled finance by enabling resource sharing, improving scale for planning, and increasing attractiveness for funders. See Box 28 for two global examples.

In India, joint municipal SWM boards in Tamil Nadu facilitate cooperation between ULGs and RLGs for comprehensive waste management. These boards allow multiple ULGs, including municipalities and town panchayats, to collaborate with nearby rural panchayats. Together, they plan, finance, and operate shared facilities such as landfills, transfer stations, and processing units. The participating local governments form joint boards or committees responsible for governance, funding, and technical decision-making associated with SWM activities across the cluster (Ministry of Urban Development 2018). In the transport space, the Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) demonstrates collaborative governance across the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region by providing a single, integrated public bus service that connects not only the central city but also satellite towns, peri-urban areas, and multiple jurisdictions under a unified operational framework (CAG 2024b). In Kerala, KUPC recommends forming Joint Planning Committees to prepare spatial development plans for larger cities and their surrounding ULGs and RLGs. Examples of such plans being discussed include Kochi and its surrounding five municipalities and five panchayats; Kozhikode with two municipalities and two panchayats; and Kottayam with two additional panchayats.

## BOX 28 | Global examples of collaborative governance frameworks

### Greater Manchester Combined Authority (UK)a

- **Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA)** unites 10 borough councils (Bolton, Bury, Manchester, Oldham, Rochdale, Salford, Stockport, Tameside, Trafford, and Wigan) under a shared governance structure headed by a directly elected Mayor.
- GMCA handles region-wide planning, regeneration, transport, housing, waste management, climate policy, and economic strategy while preserving the autonomy of each borough council. The model improves coordination, voices regional interests, and secures greater devolved powers and funding from the national government.

### Mancomunidades (Spain)b

- **A mancomunidad** is a legally created voluntary association of neighboring municipalities in Spain that collaborate to deliver services, such as water, waste management, and urban planning, that are too costly or inefficient for small towns to manage alone.
- There are over 900 such entities, which pool resources, share technical staff, and collaborate on spatial development, demonstrating a powerful model for small cities’ capacity-building.

CHAPTER 12.

# Conclusion: Realizing the NUP’s Recommendations

The chapter provides a practical roadmap for translating the NUP’s recommendations into a sequenced program of reforms. It argues that implementation must first establish strong foundations by first clearly defining the system of cities and rural-urban continuum based on current urbanization level and emerging patterns, modernizing spatial planning, reorienting public and private finance flows, and building a tiered coordination architecture across union, state, and metropolitan, city, and town levels. On this basis, the chapter outlines phased interventions, assigns coordinating actors, and aligns institutions and investments with NUP goals over time.

![img-27.jpeg](img-27.jpeg)

India is undergoing a structural transformation, and the transition to an urban economy is part of this process, as reflected in the Union Budget 2026–27’s new CERs and corridor-led infrastructure push, FC-16’s sharper urban focus and “urbanization premiums” for states that recognize and empower ULGs and create rural-to-urban transition policies, and the Economic Survey 2026’s call for 20-year spatial–economic plans that explicitly account for peri-urban belts, CTs, and economically urban large villages. Conceptually, these policies have opened the right door. However, the scale of their allocations does not match the urban challenges India faces. The next two decades will be decisive in fulfilling the dream of a Viksit Bharat by 2047. Now is the time for a flexible, forward-looking urbanization policy that aligns laws, institutions, finance, and everyday decisions with a clear vision of cities that work for people, that regenerate nature, and that help stabilize the climate, supported by a fiscal architecture that reflects today’s settlement patterns and tomorrow’s urban realities.

As this report highlights, India’s pattern of urbanization requires a greater, more holistic focus on the challenges facing existing cities, new cities, and rural areas that are rapidly becoming urban. This transition is both welcome and challenging: welcome, because it is indicative of India’s economic development, and challenging because, as this report highlights, this transition is not occurring in a well-organized, equitable, or regulated manner. Pollution, untreated waste, heat, and climate vulnerability are the increasingly problematic by-products of this transition. One core observation is the lack of policy attention paid to peri-urban areas and small towns and cities, which are experiencing the fastest rates of urbanization. However, this rapid growth often unfolds in a hidden and disorganized manner because of how we define and govern emerging urban areas. This report looks across the spectrum of urbanization—from the expansion of already large cities to the in situ urbanization of many rural areas—and details the consequences of ignoring these areas, providing suggestions on what can be done.

This chapter sets out a practical roadmap for turning the framework of recommendations for the NUP from a high-level vision into an operational, sequenced program of reforms. It argues that successful implementation hinges on first getting the foundations right, which entails clearly defining the system of cities and the rural–urban continuum based on current urbanization levels and emerging patterns of transitional urbanization, modernizing spatial and regional planning, reorienting existing and new public and private finance flows into urbanization across levels of government, and embedding a tiered coordination architecture across union, state, and metropolitan levels. Building on this scaffolding, the chapter then outlines phased interventions, assigns coordinating actors, and aligns institutions and investments with the NUP’s goals over time.

## Key stakeholders involved in developing and implementing the National Urbanization Policy

Realizing the NUP requires coordinated action across multiple levels of government, knowledge institutions, and civil society. The various actor groups play distinct but complementary roles, differentiated by their constitutional authority, fiscal leverage, technical capacity, and proximity to communities. The GoI sets national standards, fiscal incentives, and outcome benchmarks. State governments translate national frameworks into binding state-level policies, and clarify municipal mandates. ULGs and RLGs prepare plans, deliver services, engage with communities, and report on performance. Development authorities assemble land and deliver cross-boundary infrastructure in coordination with municipalities. Elected political representatives such as MLAs, MPs, Mayors, councilors, and panchayat leaders shape local priorities, spatial planning decisions, and service delivery, mediating between communities and the administration across the rural–urban continuum. Universities, research organizations, and professional bodies—particularly the TCPO, NIUA and planning schools—provide the technical scaffolding: drafting model legislation, building the next generation of planners, piloting innovations, and hosting peer learning networks. Finally, CSOs, community-based organizations (CBOs), and informal settlement dwellers’ associations bridge the gap between formal planning processes and the lived experience of communities, ensuring that reforms are participatory, transparent, and responsive to actual needs. Appendix G details the composition, responsibilities, and key contributions of each actor group.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 253

## Key transformations required for the success of the NUP

The success of the NUP will depend on the following key transformations (see Figure 55).

### Standardizing the definition and classification of statutory urban settlements and their governance arrangements across states

Standardizing the definition and classification of statutory urban settlements and aligning their governance arrangements across states is a foundational recommendation for the NUP. Without leveraging this instrument, India cannot reliably steer its urban system. This standardization can bring transformational change by correctly identifying and notifying urban settlements and creating ULGs or transitional urban bodies with defined responsibilities. States have both the legal mandate and obligation to amend municipal, panchayat, and planning laws so that settlements meeting agreed criteria such as large CTs and peri-urban belts are systematically municipalized or placed under appropriate transitional urban authorities, rather than defaulting to a “rural” classification. This measure will address the problem of hidden urbanization and ensure that accurately identified urban settlements have a recognized, statutorily empowered local government and a defined set of functions.

### Modernizing spatial and regional planning

Spatial planning and regional planning are the integrators of the NUP. They determine how infrastructure, housing, economic development, and environmental safeguards align across city regions. Mandating statutory regional plans that integrate these safeguards will create a clear, legally backed framework within which multiple actors must operate. This institutional shift will move states and municipalities away from ad hoc, project by project decisions toward rule-based allocation of land and infrastructure, which in turn will change day to day behaviors in line agencies: investments will be sequenced according to regional priorities, infrastructure corridors will be planned rather than retrospectively justified, and housing programs will be located in areas with access to jobs and services. Over time, these behavioral changes can contribute to more compact, connected, and climate resilient urban growth, especially in fast urbanizing metropolitan regions and peri-urban belts where unmanaged expansion currently drives sprawl and vulnerability.

### Reorienting existing and new public and private finance flows into urbanization across levels of government

An NUP will be credible only if it is backed by a clear, multi channel financing architecture that matches its ambitions. An NUP is not just another centrally sponsored scheme; it is a framework that should reorient how existing and new public and private finance flows into urbanization across levels of government while explicitly positioning LVC and modernized property taxation as core pillars of municipal OSR. Most urban money already moves through four channels: FC transfers, state to ULG transfers, centrally sponsored and state schemes, and a small but growing set of municipal OSRs, borrowings, and PPPs. However, these flows often do not align with where and how urbanization is actually occurring, especially in small towns, CTs and peri-urban areas.

Linking clearer functional assignments with formula-based, predictable fiscal transfers, strengthened OSRs and simplified, context-appropriate LVC instruments alters the incentives of both states and municipalities. When FC transfers and centrally sponsored schemes are partially conditioned on the adoption of NUP-aligned planning, financial management, and land-based financing standards, states are incentivized to amend municipal laws, devolve functions credibly, and invest in municipal capacity, including cadastres and property databases that can support LVC. At the city level, property tax modernization, better financial management systems, and transparent performance metrics—combined with basic LVC tools linked to statutory plans, layout approvals, and regularization—encourage municipal administrations to improve collection, bring rapidly urbanizing areas into the tax net, manage assets more systematically, and prioritize investments that deliver visible, locally grounded service and climate resilience improvements.

The use of blended finance models, such as hybrid annuity models, can complement these efforts by attracting private investment while addressing fiscal gaps in capital-intensive sectors; for example, the National Mission for Clean Ganga employs a hybrid annuity model for sewage treatment plants, combining public funding with private investment (Athar et al. 2022). Smaller towns and peri-urban areas can benefit from LVC and blended finance when these instruments are deliberately simplified and tied to their specific growth patterns rather than being designed only for metros.

## Embedding a tiered coordination architecture

The recommendations for an NUP are broad in scope, covering areas such as spatial planning, fiscal devolution, infrastructure, housing, economic development, inclusive growth, environmental protection, climate resilience, and governance reform within India’s diverse urban system. However, without a clear framework that outlines how these elements are interconnected and who should coordinate which aspects—and importantly, when this coordination is necessary—such ambition may lead to inaction. Central to this framework is the creation of urbanization councils as the primary coordination platforms for urbanization policy at the national and

state levels. At the national level, a National Urbanization Council (NUC) should be established to drive horizontal coordination among ministries on issues that cross sectoral boundaries and require union level alignment: setting NUP priorities and standards, resolving inter-ministerial conflicts on urbanization, aligning centrally sponsored schemes and FC incentives with NUP goals, and conducting quarterly reviews. This is coordination intensive because urbanization decisions cut across the finance, commerce, labor, environment, transport, energy, and social sectors, whose incentives are not automatically aligned. Between the GoI and states, the NUP should rely primarily on a structured vertical relationship of standard setting, steering, and performance oversight rather than a permanent joint coordination forum.

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 255

MoHUA should set national standards on subjects within its domain in the GoI, provide technical guidance, draft model legislation, and link fiscal transfers and scheme design to adoption of core NUP principles, while states translate these frameworks into state urbanization strategies, adapt guidelines to local contexts, adopt model legislation, and oversee on-the-ground implementation. This is a relationship of norm setting, capacity building, and performance monitoring, not continuous joint decision-making, which keeps coordination proportionate to the needs of each reform area. At the state level, State Urbanization Councils (SUCs) should be set up, convened by the state urban development departments to align sectoral departments (transport, housing, industry, environment, rural development, finance) so that a single statutory regional plan becomes the shared reference for all major investments, regulatory decisions, and scheme designs, rather than each department following its own spatial logic.

The proposed implementation framework (see Box 29) rests on a central insight: not all aspects of the NUP require the same coordination architecture (this is explained in detail in Tables 23 and 24 for key transformations). Rather than imposing a uniform, top-down coordination machine, successful implementation hinges on a functional differentiation that matches coordination mechanisms to the specific nature of each reform. Some reforms require horizontal coordination at the union level; others require vertical alignment between MoHUA and states; still others succeed primarily through steering and legislative change, with coordination playing a secondary role. Getting this granularity right is the difference between coordination structures that enable implementation and bureaucratic overhead that delays it.

## Building sectoral reforms on functional foundations

Sectoral reforms under the NUP must build on functional foundations underpinned by the basic working architecture of urban governance: clear mandates for municipalities, regional plans that guide development, predictable finance, and robust data and accountability systems. Infrastructure, housing, and economic development reforms hinge on empowered municipalities operating within coherent regional plans, with states ensuring compliance and the India Urban Observatory monitoring results. Beyond ULG capacity and finance, India needs district and metropolitan planning institutions that integrate rural, peri-urban, and urban functions; metropolitan authorities that bring fast-urbanizing villages into statutory plans; and synchronized roles for panchayats, municipalities, DPCs, and MPCs. These components will collectively ensure that emerging urban spaces are equipped with timely, region-scale services and infrastructure.

Central missions—such as AMRUT 2.0, Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0, Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban, and new frameworks such as the Cities as Growth Hubs supported by the Urban Challenge Fund—should reward project proposals aligned with regional strategies through faster approvals and higher cost sharing, fostering coordination through incentives. Economic development thrives when spatial, infrastructural, and housing priorities are integrated through regional planning, supported—not directed—by the GoI’s policies on industry, labor, and skills. Climate and environmental resilience demand city-region collaboration on airshed and watershed adaptation strategies, but their implementation remains a municipal mandate. Effective governance depends on functional devolution: clear assignments of planning, fiscal, and service responsibilities, backed by capacity building, transparency, and fiscal reform that grants predictable resources and incentives. Finally, building a national urban data ecosystem is vital. This involves embedding digital and data systems as the backbone of planning, finance, and accountability, with shared standards and interoperability enabling integrated, evidence-based urban governance.

## Aligning urban politics with reform incentives

This transformation recognizes that urban reform will move at scale only if the everyday incentives of councilors, MLAs, and other elected actors are aligned with the NUP’s rules-based planning, finance, and service delivery architecture. It treats politics not as a constraint to be avoided but as a field to be reshaped through institutional design, fiscal conditionalities, and local democratic forums. Aligning urban politics with reform incentives requires embedding core NUP principles in durable state legislation and rules, backed by independent oversight bodies (such as the NUC and SUCs). Conditional and performance-based grants should directly link visible improvements to the actions of local representatives. For example, a state-level urban incentive fund could release additional untied grants to wards that meet agreed benchmarks on property tax coverage, service quality in low-income neighborhoods, or implementation of climate resilient drainage plans, with results publicly displayed ward-wise. Similarly, MLAs whose constituencies achieve time bound targets on regularizing informal layouts or expanding inclusive public transport could gain priority access to state co-financing for major projects. Empowered ward-scale forums should become the primary arena in which elected representatives negotiate land use, infrastructure, and climate-sensitive priorities transparently. Rules-based decision-making needs to be politically safer than ad hoc interventions, especially for representatives serving vulnerable groups. This means pairing new planning and fiscal rules with tangible protections and benefits. For example, a city could adopt

256 | WRI-INDIA.ORG

a standard “no eviction without rehabilitation” protocol that ensures in situ or nearby rehousing for informal settlements along new transport corridors, combined with priority access to piped water and street lighting for those neighborhoods. Councilors who champion adherence to this protocol would then be able to demonstrate both improved services and reduced conflict, strengthening their electoral incentives to defend the rules. Continuity of reform across political cycles should be anchored in state urbanization strategies and cross-party platforms. Finally, sustained capacity building and peer learning for councilors and MLAs are essential to reframe rules-based planning, fiscal reform, and climate action as electorally rewarding, not risky.

## Supporting knowledge exchange and local innovation

Experience from Indian cities shows that some of the most effective solutions emerge from city-led experimentation long before they are reflected in national or state policy documents. Urban employment programs such as the leveraging of Kerala’s Ayyankali Urban Employment Guarantee to provide 100 days of unskilled labor work for urban poor households, including women; focusing on public asset creation and NbS in cities such as Kochi; and ULG led health outreach initiatives such as the Dhanvantari Rath mobile clinics during COVID 19 in Ahmedabad demonstrate that empowered city governments can design context specific responses at speed and scale. However, the spread of such practices remains uneven and ad hoc, often depending on a handful of proactive officials, leaders or CSOs rather than on durable, institutionalized learning channels. The NUP’s proposed urban data architecture, the ecosystem of knowledge and technical partners, offers a natural foundation for a more intentional knowledge exchange framework. Universities, research organizations, and professional bodies—along with platforms that have documented models such as Odisha’s JAGA, urban employment pilots, and city led health innovations—can move beyond one off studies to host structured peer learning networks, challenge funds, and communities of practice that cut across states, town size classes, and sectors. CSOs and CBOs, including slum dweller federations and informal worker collectives, can serve as critical intermediaries in documenting, translating, and scaling these local innovations in ways that remain grounded in lived realities. Equally important is the creation of “subaltern” knowledge flows, in which successful experiments in SMTs and peri-urban areas feed back into national guidance, state legislation, and scheme design rather than only the other way around. Periodic national and state level reviews—anchored in the India Urban Observatory and the proposed urbanization councils—can explicitly reserve space for city- and community-generated

## Phased implementation

### Phase I: Key transformations—Getting the scaffolding right

The first phase establishes the conditions for all subsequent reforms. It is anchored in three interrelated transformations: defining and governing the system of cities, modernizing spatial and regional planning, and reorienting existing and new public and private finance flows into urbanization across levels of government (see Figure 56). The fourth transformation—embedding coordination structures—applies to all three levels of government, and Table 24 discusses the different coordination approaches for each level.

### Phase II: Build sectoral reforms on functional foundations

Once the scaffolding of Phase I is in place, sectoral reforms can proceed with clarity about which coordination mechanisms to invoke. Functional foundations include empowered municipalities working within statutory regional and district plans, backed by predictable finance, robust data, and clear accountability (see Figure 57).

Infrastructure and housing reforms, for instance, do not require new coordination machinery. They rely on municipalities aligned with regional plans, with states enforcing planning compliance, and with the National Urban Observatory tracking outcomes. GoI schemes (AMRUT 2.0, Smart Cities, housing missions) should mandate that project proposals demonstrate consistency with regional plans, with fast-track approvals and higher cost sharing for compliant cities. This incentivizes coordination without imposing it.

Economic development, as the NUP notes, is not a separate silo. It succeeds when aligned with spatial planning, infrastructure, and housing. This alignment is achieved primarily through regional plans and municipal implementation, not through inter-agency committees. The GoI's role is to ensure that industrial policy, labor policy, and skills policy are aware of and support the spatial and sectoral priorities that cities identify through regional planning.

Climate and environmental action require regional coordination because hazards—flooding, heat, and pollution—cross municipal boundaries and affect interconnected populations and ecosystems. This is where city-region authorities and state agencies must coordinate around airshed, watershed, and climate adaptation strategies. However, implementation is primarily municipal: heat action plans, waste management, water supply, and NbS all depend on ULG capacity and accountability.

Governance and capacity reforms are essential for ULGs. However, they succeed through functional devolution, not broad committee-based coordination. Clear assignment of planning, financial management, service delivery, and environmental responsibilities to ULGs, coupled with capacity-building, transparency, and performance metrics from the National Urban Observatory, enables municipalities to act effectively.

Fiscal devolution and municipal finance reform are crucial because they are the instruments that give the institutions responsible for local-level NUP implementation the minimum predictable resources and incentives needed to act on their mandates; without them, even the best-designed spatial, governance, and sectoral reforms cannot be realized at scale. See Box 25 in Chapter 11 for a detailed discussion of land monetization and LVC as significant sources of OSR.

At the core, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) leads the exercise: it develops a national definitional framework (for example, drawing on approaches such as DEGURBA), specifies criteria for declaration and denotification, and sets out model governance arrangements and thresholds for different categories of settlements. States then adapt and operationalize this framework by amending their municipal, panchayat, and planning laws, deciding which state authority formally declares urban status, and aligning state level classifications, revenue assignments, and functional devolution with the new categories. | The coordination required is largely steered by MoHUA and the National Urbanization Council (NUC), supplemented with structured vertical alignment. MoHUA and the proposed NUC agree upon the national framework and timelines, consult key ministries and technical agencies, and then work with State Urbanization Councils (SUCs) to translate these standards into state legislation, administrative procedures, and data sharing arrangements, with the national urban data architecture providing the common evidence base and tracking where criteria are met. Coordination with the Office of the Registrar General is essential to harmonize statistical definitions with administrative categories, while periodic engagement with ULG associations, research organizations, and civil society helps surface anomalies (for example, large “Census Towns” still governed as rural areas) and implementation challenges.  |
|  Modernizing spatial and regional planning | **GoI level** - MoHUA (with the TCPO and other technical wings): Issues model town and country planning laws, updated URDPFI type guidance, and standards on integrating land use, transport, housing, and environment; and links central schemes and incentives to compliance with these standards. - NITI Aayog/national expert bodies: Provide policy backing and technical recommendations, and help design national challenge funds or support programs for states.**State level** - State Urban Development/Town and Country Planning Departments: drive amendments to state planning acts, and mandate statutory regional plans - SUCs (or equivalent apex committees): align multiple departments (transport, housing, environment, industries, finance) around the new planning framework and resolve conflicts.**Regional and local level** - Urban local governments (Municipal Corporations, councils, Nagar Panchayats): Become the primary statutory planning authorities at the city level, preparing and enforcing plans consistent with state law.**City-region/metropolitan planning authorities and development authorities** - Prepare and implement regional and subregional plans, manage cross-boundary infrastructure, and coordinate multiple ULGs—ideally as coordinating and implementing agencies under a municipal anchored planning framework, not as parallel planners. | **GoI–state: structured vertical steering, not joint planning** MoHUA and national bodies set standards and provide technical and financial support; states retain constitutional planning powers and adapt these into their own acts and institutions. **Intrastate (horizontal and vertical) coordination** SUCs and state TCP departments coordinate horizontally across sectoral departments (transport, housing, industry, environment, rural development) so that regional plans become the common reference for investments and regulations. **Regional and local level: Functional, problem driven coordination** Metropolitan and city-region platforms (MPCs, DPCs, or regional development authorities) coordinate municipalities, utilities, and development authorities on cross-boundary issues—transport networks, water sources, waste systems, floodplains—using statutory regional plans and shared data as anchors. Coordination here is regular but tightly scoped, with municipalities retaining democratic accountability for local zoning and development control.  |

Beyond ULG capacity reforms and financial devolution, India needs institutional arrangements that treat urbanization as a regional phenomenon. Sectoral reforms must be anchored in strengthened district and metropolitan planning institutions that jointly plan rural, peri-urban, and urban areas, so that economic transitions from farm to nonfarm work are matched by spatial planning, infrastructure, and services. Metropolitan and city region bodies—such as empowered MPCs or HMDA-type authorities—should prepare statutory regional plans with peri urban zoning, integrate transport backbones and trunk infrastructure, and bring fast-urbanizing villages, CTs, and new townships under a single governance and planning framework. At the same time, clearer functional alignment among panchayats, municipalities, DPCs, and MPCs is needed so that responsibilities for land use, service delivery, and climate resilience in transitional areas are synchronized rather than fragmented, allowing weaker local bodies to be systematically supported by stronger regional institutions.

A credible NUP requires a parallel transformation in how Indian cities generate, share, and use data. Urban governance today remains only weakly evidence based, despite the proliferation of digital systems in cities and states. The NUP should therefore position digital and data reforms not as add-ons but as core enablers of planning, investment, and accountability. This begins with a national urban data architecture that sets common standards for indicators, metadata, and interoperability across planning, service delivery, finance, climate, and mobility domains, building on existing initiatives such as national data platforms, urban data exchanges, and city-level command and control centers. These standards must be backed by protocols for routine cross-sectoral data sharing between regional, municipal, and local planning authorities, utilities, and parastatals, so that information on land use, infrastructure, environmental risk, and social conditions can be analyzed together rather than in silos.

## Phase III: Ongoing refinement

These elements are important but rely heavily on the earlier reforms, and can be framed as phased ongoing refinements rather than immediate preconditions:

- Fine-grained design of sectoral standards and technical codes (e.g., detailed building retrofitting norms, advanced TOD toolkits, specialized green construction codes) can follow once core planning and governance mandates are in place, to avoid design in a vacuum.
- More experimental or place-specific instruments (e.g., urban challenge funds for innovation, special metropolitan fiscal instruments, sophisticated LVC tools) will work better when data systems, classifications, and regional plans are functioning, and local capacity is stronger.

## Phase IV: Long-term systemic reforms

“Aligning urban politics with reform incentives” and “Supporting knowledge exchange and local innovation” are best understood as long-term, system-shaping reforms that must run alongside the scaffolding of the other phases rather than being front-loaded themselves. Table 25 discusses the different coordination approaches for each reform.

**Aligning urban politics with reform incentives:** This reform concerns reshaping how councilors, MLAs, and other elected actors perceive their interests in relation to settlement classification, planning, fiscal devolution, and enforcement. This cannot be completed in Phase I because political incentives shift only after basic building blocks—clear functional assignments, transparent fiscal rules, visible performance metrics, and some service gains—are in place and have gained credibility. Trust in new rules (for example, classification norms, ward committees with real functions, land-based revenues) builds over multiple electoral cycles and requires evidence that supporting reforms brings votes, not just administrative approval.

### Supporting knowledge exchange and local innovation:

This reform seeks to turn scattered city level experiments into a continuous, institutionalized learning system. It goes beyond creating data platforms and issuing one-off toolkits. Phase I must first establish the minimum data architecture, basic reporting routines, and institutional anchors (urban observatory, councils, technical partners) on which a serious learning ecosystem can rest. The most useful innovations often arise in response to how Phase I, II, and III reforms are experienced locally; those lessons emerge over time and require mechanisms to capture, compare, and adapt them.

## Conclusion

India’s widespread and accelerating urbanization is now firmly recognized as a defining national transition—one with profound implications for economic growth, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. Against this backdrop, the evidence-based recommendations for an NUP provide not just a response but a framework for steering this transformation coherently across an increasingly complex and planetary urban system.

The NUP is transformative precisely because it is not a single intervention. It is a system of interrelated reforms spanning spatial planning, fiscal federalism, infrastructure, housing, economic development, environmental sustainability, climate resilience, governance, and finance. Implementation requires moving beyond ad hoc projects to systematic, sequenced, coordinated action—but “coordinated” does not mean everything coordinated by everyone at all times.

Three trade-offs are particularly important for the NUP’s implementation: central steering versus local flexibility, standardization versus experimentation, and speed versus participation. The implementation roadmap set out here leans toward a model in which the GoI provides clear outcome benchmarks, minimum standards, and data architectures, while states and ULGs retain flexibility over instruments, sequencing, and institutional design within this framework. In other words, central steering is exercised through model laws, standards, incentives, and transparency rather than detailed micromanagement.

On standardization versus experimentation, the framework supports a limited number of common national standards—for example on settlement classification, core spatial planning requirements and basic fiscal reporting—combined with intentional space for state- and city-level pilots in areas such as LVC, climate budgeting, or participatory planning. Lessons from these pilots can then inform periodic revisions of guidance and standards, which is preferable to attempting to design highly specific, uniform toolkits in advance.

On speed versus participation, the approach acknowledges that India’s urbanization pressures demand timely decisions but argues that systematically embedding participation into planning and implementation cycles can improve both legitimacy and effectiveness. This does not imply exhaustive consultation on every technical detail; rather, it calls for predictable moments where communities, especially including those in informal settlements, small towns, and peri-urban areas, can shape priorities and monitor implementation, with timelines adjusted where necessary but not indefinitely deferred.

Implementation pathways will necessarily differ across India's system of cities. For megacities and large metropolitan regions, the NUP's emphasis on regional planning, city-region coordination bodies, and complex infrastructure integration is particularly salient; here, the immediate priority is often to rationalize overlapping parastatals and manage high-stakes investments at scale. For smaller cities and CTs, by contrast, the most binding constraints are frequently basic staffing, adequate finances and financial management, and the absence of simple, enforceable spatial plans; in these contexts, a lighter-touch regional planning framework accompanied by targeted capacity building and simplified fiscal instruments may be more appropriate as first steps.

State–ULG relations also vary significantly, and the implementation framework should be read with these differences in mind. In states where municipal planning powers have already been substantially devolved and development authorities work under municipal oversight, the NUP can reinforce and clarify existing good practice by aligning fiscal incentives and data systems with those arrangements. Where state legislation continues to concentrate planning authority in parastatals or retains strong discretionary control over municipal finances, the early phases of NUP implementation will need to focus on legal reform, functional clarity, and gradual rebalancing of mandates, recognizing that these changes are inherently political and may proceed unevenly across states.

Finally, NUP implementation is conceived here as an adaptive and iterative process rather than a one-time rollout. The phased approach—key transformations as foundational enablers, sectoral reforms, ongoing refinement, and long-term systemic reforms—should be complemented by explicit feedback loops in which evidence from state and city implementation feeds back into national policy. In practical terms, periodic national and state level reviews, targeted evaluations, and peer learning platforms can be used not only to adjust instruments and coordination arrangements but also to revise NUP priorities and action areas at defined intervals. This adaptive stance recognizes that India's urbanization patterns, climate risks, and economic structures will continue to evolve, and that any NUP will remain credible only if it is periodically recalibrated in light of real world implementation experience, especially from smaller cities, peri-urban areas, and rapidly transforming rural regions.

This mapping allowed us to see the gaps, particularly as they related to environmental sustainability; identify additional scope for the NUP thematic areas as requested by the ToR; and to sharpen our research questions. Five of the 10 research questions do not map to typical NUP thematic areas but do pertain to city governance and finance, as shown in Table B-2.

The National Urban Policy Framework (2018) was developed by a committee formed by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), Government of India, to create an integrated policy framework for urban development. It introduced and emphasized new themes, including environmental sustainability, climate adaptation, and mitigation, and focused more on understanding human capital and social inclusion. These themes (see Table B-3) are also aligned with global priorities in NUPs from across the world (OECD, UN-Habitat, and UNOPS 2021; OECD and UN-Habitat 2024).

## Appendix C. Multistakeholder Consultations Conducted for Framing the Draft National Urbanization Policy

Three national-level consultations were conducted to frame the policy challenges and recommendations for the draft National Urbanization Policy (NUP).

In the first consultative workshop held in New Delhi on July 6, 2022, the participants deliberated on three key questions: why should we have an NUP when "urban" is a state subject and when states urbanize at different rates? What important drivers and challenges of urbanization should an NUP address? What are the pathways to achieving inclusive and equitable economic growth, and low-carbon, climate resilient urbanization?

The first workshop discussed the key policy areas to be addressed in the draft NUP.

In the second consultative workshop, held in Bengaluru on September 12, 2022, we focused on the key policy challenges to be addressed in the NUP, elaborating on each key theme and policy objectives to be addressed under each theme and outlining the strategies, pathways, and policy objectives.

The third consultative workshop was held on July 17, 2023, as a roundtable session in WRI's flagship event, Connect Karo 2023. In this session, we showcased the key findings on urbanization policy challenges to fine-tune recommendations for the report, with a particular focus on wicked policy problems as posed by peri-urban areas (the missing middle), Census Towns (which represent urbanization without municipalization), negative externalities due to a lack of regional planning perspective and infrastructure-integrated urban development, informalization of the urban economy through insecure, low-paying jobs, cross-sectoral policy linkages, and co-benefits of climate action with sustainable development in cities.

**Insights Research Symposium, 2024.** Apart from the three national-level conferences, we also presented findings from the research on different themes conducted for the draft report on recommendations for an NUP at the Insights Research Symposium held on July 1 and 2, 2024, at New Delhi. The purpose of the Insights Research Symposium was to engage with the larger ecosystem to understand the ongoing and upcoming research planned by WRI India's peers in programming areas of interest to the organization and gauging synergies for collaborations and funding opportunities.

This was the first research symposium organized by the Cities Research, Knowledge and Engagement (RKE) Team of WRI India, headed by Dr. Sudeshna Chatterjee, to deeply engage with researchers from the Global South to identify critical research questions that WRI India could take up to accelerate the transition of Indian cities and city regions into low-carbon, equitable, and prosperous places. The two-day symposium included seven roundtable discussions and convened 63 experts. For the full list of participants and details of the roundtable discussions, see the conference proceedings available at https://wri-india.org/sites/default/files/2025-04/INSIGHTS-2024.pdf.
