## Appendix E. Five-Year Plans

### How the Five-Year Plans (FYPs) shaped India's urbanization

**First FYP (1951–56):** Key outcomes of this plan period were the Town & Country Planning Act of 1952 and the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act of 1956. The Town Planning Organization (TPO) was set up in 1955 to formulate the First Master Plan for Delhi.

**Second FYP (1956–61):** The Second Plan enabled the creation of planning institutions, after which Master Plans for a number of cities were developed. The Central Regional and Urban Planning Organization (CRUPO) was set up to evolve a plan for the Delhi Region and to advise on the development of steel towns, river valley projects, and other matters related to urban and regional planning. Urban development authorities for the key metropolitan cities of Delhi, Mumbai, and Madras were also set up in 1957

**Third FYP (1961–66):** The Third Plan further highlighted the need for town planning and the development of industrial townships. The Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) was set up in 1962 with the merger of the erstwhile TPO and the Central Regional and Urban Planning Organization (CRUPO). The Model Town and Regional Planning and Development Law was passed in 1962.

**Fourth FYP (1969–74):** Policies in this period sought to balance urban economic development by focusing on the development of smaller towns and cities. The Housing and Urban Development Corporation (1970) was formed to fund housing and urban development programs. The Environmental Improvement of Urban Slums scheme (1972) was introduced to move away from slum clearance toward slum improvement.

**Fifth FYP (1974–79):** The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act of 1976 introduced measures to control land prices in cities. The Integrated Urban Development Program (1975) developed a focus on basic services for cities and towns. The focus on small and medium towns continued and was strengthened through the Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns scheme (1979).

**Sixth FYP (1980–85):** The focus on small towns and urban infrastructure continued in the sixth FYP.

**Seventh FYP (1985–1990):** It recognized the need for involving the private sector in housing construction, and the National Housing Bank was set up in 1987 to expand the base of housing finance. For the first time, the problems of the urban poor were directly addressed through the Urban Basic Services for the Poor scheme set up by the Ministry of Urban Development in 1985, as also the National Commission on Urbanization.

**Eighth FYP (1992–1997):** For the first time, there was explicit recognition of the importance of the urban areas for the national economy and the need to devolve functions to the urban local governments (ULGs), which was enabled by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (CAA) of 1992.

A centrally sponsored scheme for the infrastructural development of megacities, called the Mega City Scheme, was launched in 1993 to tackle the problems of the biggest cities. Further, Urban Development Plan Formulation and Implementation (UDPFI) Guidelines were formulated in 1996.

**Ninth FYP (1997–2002):** The post-economic liberalization period focused on urban reforms to enhance the self-financing capacity of ULGs, provide housing for the poor, and attract Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). In 2002, the central government permitted 100 percent FDI in developing integrated townships, including housing. The National Housing and Habitat Policy (1998) and the Draft National Slum Policy (1999) emphasized government involvement in social housing for the urban poor.

**Tenth FYP (2002–2007):** It promoted market-friendly urban reforms and public-private partnerships for urban infrastructure, emphasizing that budgetary support alone is insufficient. The Plan advocated reforms in property tax, user charges, nontax revenues, and establishment cost control; better municipal asset utilization; and improved accounting systems. It also led to the launch of JnNURM.

**Eleventh FYP (2007–2012):** It focused on increasing the efficiency and productivity of cities by deregulation and development of land, and focusing on private-sector participation in infrastructure, water and sanitation, urban transport, and so on. JnNURM continued to be the main vehicle for raising infrastructure and utilities in the existing cities.

**Twelfth FYP (2012–2017):** Envisioned the inclusive, equitable, and sustainable growth of towns and cities with proper civic amenities by strengthening governance and achieving true devolution to ULGs; reforms in urban planning and urban financing; capacity-building of ULGs, meeting the policy challenges of affordable housing, and encouraging rental housing for the poor.

## Appendix G. Stakeholders Responsible for Implementing an NUP

TABLE G-1 | Key NUP actors and their roles

|  TYPE OF ACTOR | DETAILED DESCRIPTION | ROLE  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  National Government | - MoHUA (convenor) - Ministry of Finance - Ministry of Commerce and Industry - Ministry of Labour and Employment - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change - Ministry of Jal Shakti - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways - Ministry of Power - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment - Ministry of Women and Child Development - Ministry of Skills Development and Entrepreneurship - NITI Aayog - Technical experts - Civil society representatives | The national government sets the policy framework, and steers implementation by providing fiscal incentives, commissioning research, building capacity, and establishing national outcome benchmarks, data standards, and minimum safeguards while allowing states and cities discretion over instruments. Its primary responsibilities in realizing the NUP are as follows: - Develop and communicate the national vision; create and chair a National Urbanization Council (NUC). - Standardize definitions of urban and criteria for municipalization across states. - Draft and disseminate model legislation and national standards (revised town planning law, land-use frameworks, housing guidelines, climate resilience standards). - Provide technical support to states on implementation; work with TCPO, universities, and research institutions. - Condition Finance Commission transfers and centrally sponsored schemes on NUP compliance and functional clarity. - Oversee capacity-building, including expanded fellowship and training programs. - Convene research, evidence-building, and peer learning across states and cities. - Coordinate horizontal issues among ministries (climate action, water, energy, transport, finance) that cut across states.  |
|  State governments | - State Department of Urban Development (convenor) - Town and Country Planning department - Finance department - Industries and commerce department - Environment department - Water resources and irrigation department - Transport department - Housing development department - Rural development department - State disaster management authority - State Planning Board/equivalent - Major metro development authorities/SPVs - State Finance Commission - Technical experts - Civil society representatives | - Create mechanisms for inter-agency coordination by setting up State Urbanization Councils (SUCs). - Revise town and country planning laws to align them with national standards; mandate regional planning at the metropolitan scale. - Clarify roles and devolve functions to municipalities, ensuring that planning authority remains with municipalities. - Establish state urbanization strategies; allocate state funds against NUP priorities. - Build capacity in urban departments and support municipal training programs. - Monitor and report compliance with planning, housing, and environmental standards. - Adapt central guidelines and pilot innovations in their contexts.  |
|  Urban and Rural Local Governments (ULGs and RLGs) | Local governance structures for all metropolitan, non-metropolitan cities, and small towns across the rural–urban continuum | Several NUP recommendations must be implemented by ULGs and RLGs within their jurisdictions. Their responsibilities include the following: - Participate in regional planning processes; adopt and enforce regional plans in local zoning and development controls. - Deliver basic services (water, sanitation, waste, transport) aligned with spatial plans and housing strategy. - Collect property taxes and user fees; manage municipal finances transparently. - Prepare and implement local climate action and resilience plans. - Engage communities in planning and implementation; support in situ upgrading of informal settlements. - Report to the national data platforms on service delivery, revenue, and performance metrics. - Work with development authorities on land assembly and serviced-land delivery; manage land-use and housing implementation.  |

Equitable, productive, low-carbon and resilient system of cities in India | 275

TABLE G-1 | Key NUP actors and their roles (Cont'd)

|  TYPE OF ACTOR | DETAILED DESCRIPTION | ROLE  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Elected political representatives | Elected political representatives include MLAs, MPs, mayors, councilors, and panchayat leaders. They mediate between communities and the administration across the rural–urban continuum, including city cores, small towns, and peri-urban areas. | MLAs and MPs influence state-level legislation, scheme design and budget allocations; mayors and councilors in ULGs shape local priorities, spatial planning decisions, and service delivery; and panchayat representatives in transitional areas where urbanization is not yet formally recognized influence decisions on infrastructure and service delivery. Political actors are needed to • champion key NUP reforms, such as settlement reclassification, statutory regional plans, and property tax modernization; • shape local implementation of spatial planning, building permissions, and infrastructure projects, especially in fast-urbanizing peripheries where unregulated construction and environmental stress are most acute; • work with ward committees and other participatory forums to aggregate citizen demands, negotiate trade-offs, and institutionalize climate-sensitive priorities in local plans and budgets aligned with NUP incentives; and • respond to fiscal and regulatory incentives embedded in NUP-aligned schemes (for example, conditional grants and performance frameworks), creating political backing for reforms that expand predictable, rule-based municipal finance and strengthen local institutions.  |
|  Development authorities |  | These are parastatal bodies charged with land assembly, trunk infrastructure, and implementation across jurisdictions. Their roles are as follows: • Prepare and enforce regional and sub-regional spatial plans in coordination with regional local governance units, not separately. • Assemble land through town planning schemes, pooling, and other mechanisms for public amenities and infrastructure. • Deliver trunk infrastructure (water, waste, power, transport) aligned with regional plans. • Partner with municipalities on integrated land-use and service delivery. • Use value-capture tools to finance growth-related infrastructure. • Conduct periodic assessments of peri-urban needs and infrastructure gaps.  |
|  Knowledge and technical partners | Universities, research organizations, and professional bodies | Universities, research organizations, and professional bodies such as TCPO, NIUA, and NIDM play the following essential roles: • Draft model legislation and technical guidance; provide continuous research on planning innovations and capacity gaps. • Build the next generation of planners, engineers, and governance professionals through curriculum redesign and partnerships with ULGs and state bodies. • Pilot new approaches (regional planning frameworks, land-use integration, technology deployment) and document learnings. • Conduct systematic studies on city classification, capacity assessments, migration, and climate vulnerability mapping. • Host peer learning networks and communities of practice across states and cities.  |
|  Civil society | CSOs, NGOs, and community-based organizations (CBOs) | • They are essential force multipliers. The Odisha JAGA model illustrates this: slum dwellers’ associations and CBOs shaped facility design for cyclone resilience, ensuring that implementation responded to actual community needs. Ring-fencing small shares of scheme budgets for community engagement and establishing formal grievance mechanisms within municipal bodies are low-cost moves with significant payoffs. Their roles include the following: • Co-run participatory planning sessions; translate complex regulations for affected communities. • Support social audits and citizen feedback on municipal service delivery and compliance. • Partner with ULGs on community engagement in slum upgrading, housing, and climate action. • Monitor and report on the distributional impacts of reforms—who benefits, who is displaced. • Foster community-led maintenance and stewardship of shared infrastructure, particularly blue-green assets and open spaces.  |

## About WRI India

WRI India, an independent knowledge organization registered as the India Resources Trust provides objective information and practical proposals to foster environmentally sound and socially equitable development. Through research, analysis, and recommendations, WRI India puts ideas into action to build transformative solutions to protect the earth, promote livelihoods, and enhance human well-being.

Know more: wri-india.org
